s: Eccles. 4:9–12 — “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, for he has no other to help him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have heat; but how can one be warm alone?
And if one prevails against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
Among the many reasons that may be given for the sad decline of true Christianity, perhaps our neglect to assemble ourselves together in religious societies may not be one of the least.

So that I may therefore do my part toward promoting so excellent a means of piety, I have chosen a passage of Scripture drawn from the experience of the wisest of men, which, when somewhat enlarged upon and illustrated, will fully serve my present purpose; that purpose being to show, in the best manner I can, the necessity and benefits of society in general, and of religious society in particular.
“Two are better than one,” and so on.
From these words I shall take occasion to prove,
First, the truth of the wise man's assertion, “Two are better than one,” and that with reference to society in general, and religious society in particular.
Secondly, to give some reasons why two are better than one, especially as to the last point.
1. Because men can raise one another up when they happen to slip: “For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.”
2. Because they can impart heat to each other: “Again, if two lie together, then they have heat; but how can one be warm alone?”
3. Because they can protect each other from those who oppose them: “And if one prevails against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” From this,
Thirdly, I shall take occasion to show the duty that rests upon every member of a religious society.
And fourthly, I shall draw an inference or two from what may be said, and then conclude with a word or two of exhortation.
First, I am to prove the truth of the wise man's assertion that “two are better than one,” and that with reference to society in general, and religious societies in particular.
And how can this be done better than by showing that it is absolutely necessary for the welfare of both the bodies and the souls of men?
Indeed, if we look upon man as he came out of the hands of his Maker, we imagine him to be perfect, complete, lacking nothing.
But God, whose thoughts are not as our thoughts, saw something still missing to make Adam happy.
And what was that?
Why, a helper suitable for him.
For thus the Scripture speaks: “And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make a helper suitable for him.”
Observe, God said, “It is not good,” thereby implying that the creation would have been imperfect in some sense unless a suitable helper was found for Adam.

And if this was the case of man before the fall, if a helper was fitting for him in a state of perfection, then surely since the fall—when we come naked and helpless out of our mother's womb, when our needs increase with our years, and we can scarcely survive a day without the mutual assistance of one another—well may we say, “It is not good for man to be alone.”
Society, then, as we see, is absolutely necessary with respect to our bodily and personal needs.
If we carry our view further and consider mankind as divided into different cities, countries, and nations, its necessity will appear yet more evident.
For how can communities be maintained, or commerce carried on, without society?

Certainly not at all, since Providence seems wisely to have assigned a particular product to almost every particular country, on purpose, as it were, to oblige us to be social; and has so admirably joined the parts of the whole body of mankind together “that the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; nor again the hand to the foot, I have no need of you.”
Many other instances might be given of the necessity of society with reference to our bodily, personal, and national needs.
But what are all these, when weighed in the balance of the sanctuary, in comparison with the infinitely greater need of it with respect to the soul?
It was chiefly with regard to this better part, no doubt, that God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

For let us suppose Adam to be as happy as can be, placed as lord of the creation in the paradise of God, and spending all his hours in adoring and praising the blessed Author of his being; yet, since his soul was the very copy of the divine nature, whose particular property it is to be communicative, he could not, apart from the divine all-sufficiency, be completely happy, because he was alone and had no one with whom to share himself, nor even be content in paradise, for lack of a partner in his joys.
God knew this, and therefore said, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make a helper suitable for him.”

And though this proved a fatal means of his fall, yet that was not owing to any natural consequence of society, but partly to that cursed apostate who craftily lies in wait to deceive, and partly to Adam's own folly in choosing to be miserable with one he loved rather than trust God to raise up another wife for him.

If indeed we reflect on the close fellowship our first parent could carry on with heaven in a state of innocence, we shall be inclined to think that he had as little need of society for his soul as we earlier supposed him to have for his body.

But still, since God and the holy angels were so far above him on the one hand, and the beasts so far beneath him on the other, there was nothing like having someone to converse with who was “bone of his bone, and flesh of his flesh.”
Man, then, as we see, could not be fully happy even in paradise without a companion of his own kind, much less now that he is driven out.

For let us view him a little in his natural state now, since the fall, as “having his understanding darkened, his mind alienated from the life of God”; as no more able to see the way in which he should go than a blind man is able to describe the sun; and that, notwithstanding this, he must receive his sight before he can see God; and that if he never sees him, he can never be happy.
Let us view him in this light (or rather, this darkness), and deny the necessity of society if we can.
A divine revelation, we find, is absolutely necessary, since by nature we are as unable to know our duty as we are to do it.
And how shall we learn unless someone teaches us?
But if God were to do this himself, how could we do anything but, like Moses, exceedingly quake and fear?
Nor would the ministry of angels in this matter be without too much terror.
It is necessary, therefore (at least God's dealings with us have shown it to be so), that we should be drawn with the cords of a man.

And that, a divine revelation being granted, we should use one another's assistance, under God, to instruct each other in the knowledge, and to exhort one another to the practice, of those things which belong to our everlasting peace.

This is undoubtedly the great purpose of society intended by God since the fall, and a strong argument it is why “two are better than one,” and why we should “not forsake the assembling of ourselves together.”
But further, let us consider ourselves as Christians, as having this natural veil in some measure taken from our eyes by the help of God's Holy Spirit, and so enabled to see what he requires of us.

Let us suppose that we have in some degree tasted the good word of life, and have felt the powers of the world to come influencing and molding our souls into a religious disposition; that we are fully and heartily convinced that we are soldiers enlisted under the banner of Christ, and that we proclaimed open war at our baptism against the world, the flesh, and the devil, and have perhaps frequently renewed our pledge to do so by partaking of the Lord's Supper; that we are surrounded by millions of foes without and infected with a legion of enemies within; that we are commanded to shine as lights in the world, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation; that we are traveling toward a long eternity, and need every imaginable help to show us the way and encourage us on our journey there.
Let us, I say, reflect on all this, and then how shall each of us cry out, brethren, what a necessary thing it is to meet together in religious societies?
The early Christians were fully aware of this, and therefore we find them continually keeping up fellowship with one another; for what does the Scripture say?
They continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, Acts 2:42.
Peter and John were no sooner dismissed by the great council than they hurried away to their companions.
“And being set at liberty, they came to their own people and told them all these things which the high priest had said to them,” Acts 4:23.
Paul, as soon as he was converted, “stayed three days with the disciples who were at Damascus.”
Acts 9:19. And Peter afterward, when released from prison, immediately goes to the house of Mary, where there were “great multitudes assembled, praying,” Acts 12:12.
And it is reported of the Christians in later ages that they used to assemble together before daylight to sing a psalm to Christ as God.
So precious was the Communion of Saints in those days.
If it is asked, what advantages shall we reap from such a practice now?
I answer, much in every way.

“Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor; for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, for he has no other to help him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have heat; but how can one be warm alone?
And if one prevails against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
This leads me directly to my second general head, under which I was to give some reasons why “two are better than one,” especially in religious society.

1. Since man in his present condition cannot always stand upright, but because of the frailty of his nature cannot help but fall, one outstanding reason why two are better than one—or, in other words, one great advantage of religious society—is “that when they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.”
And an excellent reason this is indeed!

For alas! When we reflect how prone we are to be drawn into error in our judgments and into vice in our practice, and how unable, or at least how very unwilling, we are to detect or correct our own failings; when we consider how ready the world is to flatter us in our faults, and how few there are kind enough to tell us the truth, what a priceless privilege it must be to have a company of true, judicious, wholehearted friends about us, continually watching over our souls, to inform us where we have fallen, and to warn us not to fall again in the future!
Surely it is such a privilege that (to use the words of an eminent Christian) we shall never know its value until we come to glory.

But this is not all; for even supposing that we could always stand upright, yet whoever reflects on the difficulties of religion in general, and on his own tendency to lukewarmness and indifference in particular, will find that he must be zealous as well as steady if he ever expects to enter the kingdom of heaven.
Here, then, the wise man points out to us another excellent reason why two are better than one:
“Again, if two lie together, then they have heat; but how can one be warm alone?”
Which was the next thing to be considered.
2. A second reason why two are better than one is that they can impart heat to each other.
It is an observation no less true than common, that burning coals, if placed apart, soon go out, but if heaped together, quicken and enliven each other and give a lasting heat.
The same holds true in the case now before us.
If Christians kindled by the grace of God unite, they will quicken and enliven each other; but if they separate and keep apart, it is no wonder if they soon grow cool or lukewarm.
If two or three meet together in Christ's name, they will have heat; but how can one be warm alone?
Observe: “How can one be warm alone?”
The wise man's expressing himself in the form of a question implies an impossibility, or at least a very great difficulty, of being warm in religion without company, where company may be had.
See here, then, another excellent benefit flowing from religious society: it will keep us zealous, as well as steady, in the way of godliness.
But let me illustrate this a little further by a comparison or two.

Let us look upon ourselves (as was hinted above) as soldiers enlisted under Christ's banner; as going out with “ten thousand to meet one who comes against us with twenty thousand”; as persons who are to “wrestle not only with flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, and spiritual wickedness in high places.”

And then tell me, all you who fear God, whether it is not an invaluable privilege to have a company of fellow soldiers continually about us, encouraging and exhorting each other to stand our ground, to keep our ranks, and manfully to follow the captain of our salvation, even though it be through a sea of blood?

Let us consider ourselves in another light mentioned before, as persons traveling toward a long eternity; as rescued in some measure by the free grace of God from our natural Egyptian bondage, and marching under the leadership of our spiritual Joshua through the wilderness of this world to the land of our heavenly Canaan.
Let us further reflect how inclined we are to be startled at every difficulty, to cry, “There are lions!
There are lions in the way!
There are the sons of Anak” to be grappled with before we can possess the promised land.

How prone we are, like Lot's wife, to look longingly back on our spiritual Sodom, or, like the foolish Israelites, to long again for the flesh-pots of Egypt, and to return to our former natural state of bondage and slavery.

Consider this, my brethren, and see what a blessed privilege it will be to have a company of true Israelites about us, always reminding us of the folly of any such cowardly intention, and of the unbearable misery we shall run into if we fall even the least short of the promised land.
More might be said on this point, if the limits of a discourse of this nature did not oblige me to hasten on,
3. To give a third reason, mentioned by the wise man in the text, why two are better than one: because they can protect each other from enemies without.
“And if one prevails against him, yet two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”

Up to now we have considered the advantages of religious societies as a great safeguard against falling (at least falling dangerously) into sin and lukewarmness, and that, too, through our own corruptions.
But what does the wise son of Sirach say?

“My son, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation”; and that not only from inward but from outward foes, particularly from those two great adversaries, the world and the devil; for no sooner will your eye be turned heavenward than the former will immediately be drawing it another way, telling you that you need not be singular in order to be religious, that you may be a Christian without going so far out of the common road.
Nor will the devil be lacking in his crafty insinuations or ungodly suggestions to divert or frighten you from pressing forward, “that you may lay hold on the crown of life.”

And if he cannot prevail this way, he will try another; and in order to make his temptation less easily detected, but at the same time more successful, he will perhaps employ some of your nearest relatives or most powerful friends (as he set Peter on our blessed Master), who will always be urging you to spare yourself, telling you that you need not take such pains, that it is not so difficult a matter to get to heaven as some people would make it, nor the way so narrow as others imagine it to be.

But see here the advantage of religious company; for supposing you find yourself thus surrounded on every side, and unable to withstand such dreadful (though seemingly friendly) counsels, hurry away to your companions, and they will teach you a truer and better lesson: they will tell you that you must be singular if you would be religious; that it is as impossible for a Christian to be hidden as for a city set upon a hill; that if you would be an almost Christian (and you might as well be none at all), you may live in the same idle, indifferent manner as you see most other people do; but if you would be not only almost but altogether a Christian, they will inform you that you must go a great deal further; that you must not only faintly seek, but “earnestly strive to enter in at the narrow gate”; that there is but one way to heaven now, as formerly, namely, through the narrow passage of a sound conversion; and that in order to bring about this mighty work, you must undergo a constant but necessary discipline of fasting, watching, and prayer.

And therefore the only reason why those friends give you such advice is that they are not willing to take such pains themselves; or, as our Savior told Peter on a similar occasion, because they “do not relish the things that are of God, but the things that are of men.”
This, then, is another excellent blessing arising from religious society: that friends can thereby protect each other from those who oppose them.
The devil is fully aware of this, and therefore he has always done his utmost to suppress and put a stop to the communion of saints.
This was his grand device at the first planting of the gospel: to persecute those who professed it, in order to separate them.
And though God, as he always will, overruled this for the better, yet it shows what hostility he has against Christians assembling themselves together.
Nor has he yet given up his old stratagem; it being his usual way to entice us off by ourselves in order to tempt us, where, being without one another's help, he hopes to lead us captive at his will.

But, on the contrary, knowing that his own interest is strengthened by society, he would first persuade us to neglect the communion of saints, and then bid us “stand in the way of sinners,” hoping thereby to bring us into the seat of the scornful.
Judas and Peter are sad examples of this.

The former had no sooner left his company at supper than he went out and betrayed his Master; and the dismal downfall of the latter, when he ventured himself among a company of enemies, plainly shows us what the devil will attempt when he gets us by ourselves.
Had Peter kept to his own company, he might have kept his integrity; but a single cord, alas! how quickly was it broken?
Our blessed Savior knew this full well, and therefore it is very noteworthy that he always sent out his disciples “two by two.”

And now, after so many advantages to be reaped from religious society, may we not very justly cry out with the wise man in my text, “Woe to him who is alone; for when he falls, he has no other to lift him up!”
When he is cold, he has no friend to warm him; when he is attacked, he has no second to help him withstand his enemy.
III. I now come to my third general head, under which were to be shown the several duties that rest upon every member of a religious society as such, which are three:
1. Mutual reproof; 2.
Mutual exhortation; 3. Mutually assisting and defending each other.
1. Mutual reproof. “Two are better than one; for when they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.”

Now, reproof may be taken either in a broader sense, and then it signifies our raising up a brother by the gentlest means when he falls into sin and error; or in a narrower meaning, as reaching no further than those failings which unavoidably happen to the holiest men living.
The wise man in the text supposes all of us subject to both: “For when they fall (thereby implying that each of us may fall), the one will lift up his fellow.”

From this we may infer that “when any brother is overtaken in a fault, he who is spiritual (that is, regenerate, and knowing the corruption and weakness of human nature) ought to restore such a one in a spirit of meekness.”
And why he should do so, the apostle adds a reason: “considering yourself, lest you also be tempted”; that is, considering your own frailty, lest you also fall by the same temptation.
We are all frail, unstable creatures; and it is owing solely to the free grace and good providence of God that we do not run into the same excess of riot as other men.

Every offending brother, therefore, has a claim on our pity rather than our resentment; and each member should strive to be the most forward, as well as the most gentle, in restoring him to his former state.
But supposing a person has not been overtaken, but has fallen willfully into a crime; yet who are you, that you deny forgiveness to your offending brother?
“Let him who stands take heed lest he fall.”
Take the holy apostles, brethren, as eminent examples to learn from how you ought to behave in this matter.
Consider how quickly they gave the right hand of fellowship to Peter, who had so willfully denied his Master; for we find John and him together only two days later, John 20:2.
And in verse 19 we find him assembled with the rest.
So soon did they forgive, so soon did they associate with their sinful yet repentant brother.
“Let us go and do likewise.”

But there is another kind of reproof that rests upon every member of a religious society; namely, a gentle rebuke for some failing or other which, though not actually sinful, may yet become an occasion of sin.

This indeed seems an easier point, but will perhaps be found a more difficult one than the former; for when a person has really sinned, he cannot but admit that his brethren's reproof is just; whereas when it is only for some small misconduct, the pride that is in our natures will scarcely allow us to bear (endure, tolerate) it.
But however unpleasant this pill may be to our brother, yet if we have any concern for his welfare, it must be administered by some friendly hand or other.
By all means, then, let it be applied; only, like a skillful physician, gild over the unpleasant pill, and endeavor, if possible, to deceive your brother into health and soundness.
“Let all bitterness, and wrath, and malice, and evil speaking be put away” from it.
Let the patient know that his recovery is the only thing aimed at, and that you take no delight in grieving your brother without cause; then you cannot fail to succeed.
2. Mutual exhortation is the second duty arising from the words of the text:
“Again, if two lie together, then they have heat.”

Observe, the wise man supposes it to be as impossible for religious persons to meet together and not be the warmer for each other's company, as for two persons to lie in the same bed and yet freeze with cold.
But now, how is it possible to communicate heat to each other without mutually stirring up the gift of God which is in us by brotherly exhortation?

Let every member of a religious society, then, write that zealous apostle's advice on the tablets of his heart: “See that you exhort and stir up one another to love and to good works; and so much the more as you see the day of the Lord approaching.”

Believe me, brethren, we need exhortation to rouse our sleepy souls, to set us on our guard against the temptations of the world, the flesh, and the devil; to move us to deny ourselves, to take up our crosses, and to follow our blessed Master and the glorious company of saints and martyrs, “who through faith have fought the good fight, and have gone before us to inherit the promises.”

A third part, therefore, of the time during which a religious society meets seems necessary to be spent in this important duty; for what does it avail to have our understandings enlightened by devout reading, unless our wills are at the same time inclined and inflamed by mutual exhortation to put it into practice?

Add also that this is the best way both to receive and to impart light, and the only means of preserving and increasing that warmth and heat which each person first brought with him; God so ordering this, as all other spiritual gifts, that “to him who has, that is, improves and shares what he has, more shall be given; but from him who has not, or does not improve the heat he has, shall be taken away even that which he seemed to have.”
So needful, so essentially necessary, is exhortation to the good of society.
3. Thirdly, the text points out another duty that rests upon every member of a religious society: to defend each other from those who oppose them.
“And if one prevails against him, yet two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
Here the wise man takes it for granted that offenses will come, yes, and that they may prevail too.
And this is no more than our blessed Master told us long ago.
Not, indeed, that there is anything in Christianity itself that has the least tendency to give rise to or promote such offenses. No; on the contrary, it breathes nothing but unity and love.

But so it is that ever since the fatal sentence pronounced by God after our first parents' fall, “I will put enmity between your seed and her seed,” he who is born after the flesh, the unregenerate, unconverted sinner, has in all ages “persecuted him who is born after the Spirit”; and so it always will be.
Accordingly, we find an early proof of this given in the instances of Cain and Abel, of Ishmael and Isaac, and of Jacob and Esau.
And indeed, the whole Bible contains little else but a history of the great and continued opposition between the children of this world and the children of God.

The first Christians were remarkable examples of this; and though those troublesome times, blessed be God, are now over, yet the apostle has laid it down as a general rule, and all who are sincere prove its truth by experience, that “those who will live godly in Christ Jesus must (to the end of the world, in some degree or other) suffer persecution.”
So that this may not make us desert our blessed Master's cause, every member should therefore unite their forces in order to stand against it.

And to accomplish this the better, each would do well from time to time to share his experiences, grievances, and temptations, and to beg his companions (first asking God's help, without which all is nothing) to give reproof, exhortation, or comfort, as his case requires; so that “if one cannot prevail against it, yet two shall withstand it; and a threefold (much less a manifold) cord will not be quickly broken.”
IV. But it is time for me to proceed to the fourth general point proposed: to draw an inference or two from what has been said.

1. And first, if “two are better than one,” and the advantages of religious society are so many and so great, then it is the duty of every true Christian to set on foot, establish, and promote, as far as lies in his power, societies of this nature.
And I believe we may venture to affirm that if ever a spirit of true Christianity is revived in the world, it must be brought about by some such means as this.

Surely motives cannot be lacking to stir us up to this commendable and necessary undertaking; for, granting that all that has been advanced so far is of no force, yet it seems to me that the single consideration that a great part of our happiness in heaven will consist in the Communion of Saints, or that the interest as well as the piety of those who differ from us is strengthened and supported by nothing more than their frequent meetings—either of these considerations, I say, one would think, should induce us to do our utmost to copy their good example, and to establish a lasting and devout communion of the saints on earth.
Add to this that we find the kingdom of darkness established daily by such means; and shall not the kingdom of Christ be set up in opposition to it?
Shall the children of Belial assemble and strengthen each other in wickedness, and shall not the children of God unite and strengthen themselves in piety?
Shall society upon society be approved for midnight revelry and the promotion of vice, and scarcely one be found intended for the spreading of virtue?
Be astonished, O heavens, at this!

2. But this leads me to a second inference; namely, to warn people of the great danger that those are in who, whether by their subscriptions, presence, or approval, promote societies of a nature quite opposite to religion.

And here I would not be understood to mean only those public gatherings which are clearly designed for nothing else but revelry and banqueting, for lewdness and wantonness, and at which a modest heathen would blush to be present; but also those seemingly innocent entertainments and gatherings which the more polite part of the world is so very fond of and spends so much time in, but which nevertheless keep as many persons from a sense of true religion as intemperance, debauchery, or any other crimes whatever.
Indeed, while we are in this world we must have proper recreation, to fit us both for the business of our calling and for religion.

But then, for persons who call themselves Christians, who have solemnly vowed at their baptism to renounce the vanities of this sinful world, who are commanded in Scripture “to abstain from all appearance of evil, and to have their citizenship in heaven”—for such persons as these to support gatherings which (to say nothing worse of them) are vain and trifling, and have a natural tendency to draw our minds away from God, is absurd, ridiculous, and sinful.
Surely two are not better than one in this case. No; it is to be wished that not one could be found involved in it.
The sooner we forsake the assembling of ourselves together in such a manner, the better; and it matters not how quickly the cord that holds such societies together (were it a thousandfold) is broken.

But you, brethren, have not so learned Christ; but, on the contrary, like true disciples of your Lord and Master, you have by the blessing of God (as this evening's solemn gathering abundantly testifies) happily formed yourselves into such societies, which, if duly attended and made good use of, cannot fail to strengthen you in your Christian warfare, and “make you fruitful in every good word and work.”

What remains for me but, as was proposed, in the first place to close what has been said with a word or two by way of exhortation, and to beseech you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to go on in the way you have begun; and by a constant, conscientious attendance at your respective societies, to discourage vice, encourage virtue, and build each other up in the knowledge and fear of God.

Only permit me to “stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance,” and to exhort you, “if there is any consolation in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit,” again and again to consider that, as all Christians in general, so all members of religious societies in particular, are in a special manner like houses built upon a hill; and that therefore it greatly concerns you to walk carefully toward those who are outside, and to take heed to yourselves that your conduct in common life is such as befits so open and distinctive a profession of the gospel of Christ; knowing that the eyes of all people are upon you, closely inspecting every circumstance of your behavior, and that every notorious, willful failing of any single member will in some measure bring scandal and dishonor upon your whole fraternity.

Labor, therefore, my beloved brethren, to let your practice match your profession; and do not think that it will be enough for you to plead at the last day, Lord, have we not assembled ourselves together in your name, and enlivened each other by singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs?

For truly, I say to you, notwithstanding this, our blessed Lord will bid you depart from him; yes, you shall receive a great condemnation if, in the midst of these great pretensions, you are found to be workers of iniquity.
But God forbid that any such evil should befall you; that there should ever be a Judas, a traitor, among such distinguished followers of our common Master.

No; on the contrary, the excellence of your rule, the regularity of your meetings, and more especially your devout zeal in assembling in such a public and solemn manner so often in the year, persuade me to think that you are willing not merely to seem, but to be in reality, Christians; and that you hope to be found at the last day to be what you would be esteemed now: holy, sincere disciples of a crucified Redeemer.
Oh, may you always continue so minded!

And make it your daily, constant endeavor, both by precept and example, to turn all your dealings with others, more especially those of your own societies, into the same most blessed spirit and temper.

Thus you will adorn the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ in all things; thus you will anticipate the happiness of a future state; and by attending upon and making good use of the communion of saints on earth, you will be made fit to join the communion and fellowship of the spirits of just men made perfect, of the holy angels, yes, of the ever blessed and eternal God in heaven.

Which may God of his infinite mercy grant through Jesus Christ our Lord; to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, three persons and one God, be ascribed, as is most due, all honor and praise, might, majesty, and dominion, now and forever. Amen.

If we ask why there is so little love to be found among Christians, why the very mark by which everyone should know that we are disciples of the holy Jesus is almost banished from the Christian world, we shall find it due, in great measure, to a neglect or superficial performance of that excellent part of prayer, intercession, or imploring the divine grace and mercy on behalf of others.

Some forget this duty of praying for others because they seldom remember to pray for themselves; and even those who are constant in praying to their Father who is in heaven are often so selfish in their addresses to the throne of grace that they do not enlarge their petitions for the welfare of their fellow Christians as they ought; and so they fall short of attaining that Christian charity, that sincere love for their brothers, which their sacred profession obliges them to aspire to, and without which, though they should give all their goods to feed the poor, and even give their bodies to be burned, it would profit them nothing.
Since these things are so, I shall from the words of the text (though they were originally intended in a narrower sense) endeavor to show,
I. First, that it is every Christian's duty to pray for others as well as for himself.
II. Secondly, whom we ought to pray for, and in what manner we should do it. And,
III. Thirdly, I shall offer some motives to stir up all Christians to abound in this great duty of intercession.
I. First, I shall endeavor to show that it is every Christian's duty to pray for others, as well as for himself.

Now prayer is a duty founded on natural religion; even the heathen never neglected it, though many Christian heathen among us do; and it is so essential to Christianity that you might as reasonably expect to find a living man without breath as a true Christian without the spirit of prayer and supplication.
Thus, no sooner was St. Paul converted than "behold, he prays," says the Lord Almighty.
And so it will be with every child of God as soon as he becomes one, for prayer is truly called the natural cry of the newborn soul.
For in the heart of every true believer there is a heavenly tendency, a divine attraction, which draws him to converse with God as perceptibly as the magnet attracts the needle.

A deep sense of their own weakness and of Christ's fullness, a strong conviction of their natural corruption and of the necessity of renewing grace, will not let them rest from crying day and night to their Almighty Redeemer, that the divine image, which they lost in Adam, may through his all-powerful mediation, and the sanctifying work of his blessed Spirit, be begun, carried on, and fully perfected both in their souls and bodies.

So earnest, so persistent are all sincere Christians in praying for themselves; but then, not having so lively, lasting, and deep a sense of the needs of their Christian brothers, they are for the most part too negligent and deficient in their prayers for them.

Whereas, if the love of God were poured out in our hearts, and if we loved our neighbor in the way in which the Son of God our Savior loved us, and according to his command and example, we could not help being as persistent for their spiritual and temporal welfare as for our own, and as earnestly desiring and striving that others should share in the benefits of the death and passion of Jesus Christ as we ourselves.

Let no one think that this is an uncommon degree of charity, a high pitch of perfection which not everyone can attain; for if we are all commanded to "love our neighbor (that is, every man) even as ourselves," and even to "lay down our lives for the brothers," then it is the duty of all to pray for their neighbors as much as for themselves, and by every possible act and expression of love and affection toward them, at all times, to show their readiness even to lay down their lives for them, if it should ever please God to call them to it.

Our blessed Savior, as "he has set us an example, that we should follow his steps" in everything else, has done so more especially in this; for in that divine, that perfect and inimitable prayer (recorded in John 17) which he offered just before his passion, we find only a few petitions for his own welfare, though many for his disciples'; and in that perfect form which he has been pleased to prescribe for us, we are taught to say, not "my," but "our Father," to remind us that whenever we approach the throne of grace, we ought to pray not for ourselves alone, but for all our brothers in Christ.
Intercession, then, is certainly a duty binding on all Christians.
II. Whom we are to intercede for, and how this duty is to be performed, is next to be considered.
1. And first, our intercession must be universal.
"I desire (says the apostle) that prayers, supplications, and intercessions be made for all men."

For as God's mercy is over all his works, and as Jesus Christ died to redeem a people out of all nations and languages, so we should pray that "all men may come to the knowledge of the truth and be saved."

Many precious promises are made in Holy Scripture that the gospel shall be proclaimed through the whole world, that "the earth shall be covered with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea"; and therefore it is our duty not to confine our petitions to our own nation, but to pray that all those nations who now sit in darkness and in the shadow of death may have the glorious gospel shine out upon them as well as upon us.

But you do not need anyone to teach you this, since you yourselves are taught by God, and by Jesus Christ himself, to pray that his kingdom may come; part of the meaning of which petition is that "God's ways may be known upon earth, and his saving power among all nations."

2. Next to praying for all men, we should, according to St. Paul's rule, pray for kings, particularly for our present sovereign King George, and all who are placed in authority under him, that we may lead quiet lives in all godliness and honesty.

For if we consider how heavy the burden of government is, and how much the welfare of any people depends on the zeal and godly conduct of those who rule over them; if we set before us the many dangers and difficulties to which governors are exposed by their position, and the continual temptations they are under to luxury and self-indulgence, we shall not only pity them but pray for them: that he who preserved Esther, David, and Josiah "unspotted from the world" amid the grandeur of a court, and gave success to their plans, would also preserve them holy and blameless, and prosper all the works of their hands upon them. But
3. Thirdly, you ought in a more special manner to pray for those whom "the Holy Spirit has made overseers over you."

This is what St. Paul asks again and again of the churches to which he writes. He says in the text, "Brothers, pray for us"; and again, in his letter to the Ephesians, "praying always, with every kind of supplication; and for me also, that I may open my mouth boldly to declare the mystery of the gospel."

And in another place, to express his earnestness in this request and the great importance of their prayers for him, he bids the church "strive (or, as the original word signifies, be in agony) together with him in their prayers."

And surely, if the great St. Paul, that chosen vessel, that favorite of heaven, needed the most persistent prayers of his Christian converts, much more do the ordinary ministers of the gospel stand in need of the intercession of their respective flocks.

And I must insist on this branch of your duty in a more special manner, because it is a matter of such importance; for no doubt much good is often withheld from many because they neglect to pray for their ministers, good which they would have received had they prayed for them as they ought.
Not to mention that people often complain of the lack of diligent and faithful pastors.
But how do they deserve good pastors who will not earnestly pray to God for such?
If we will not pray to the Lord of the harvest, can it be expected that he will send out laborers into his harvest?
Besides, what ingratitude it is not to pray for your ministers!
For shall they watch and labor in the word and doctrine for you and your salvation, and shall you not pray for them in return?
If anyone bestows favors on your bodies, you think it right, fitting, and your binding duty to pray for them; and shall they not be remembered in your prayers who daily feed and nourish your souls?
Add to all this that praying for your ministers will be a clear proof that you believe that though Paul plants and Apollos waters, it is God alone who gives the increase.

And you will also find it the best means you can use to promote your own welfare, because God, in answer to your prayers, may impart a double portion of his Holy Spirit to them, by which they will be qualified to deal out to you larger measures of knowledge in spiritual things, and be enabled more skillfully to divide the word of truth.

If people would only constantly observe this direction, and when their ministers are praying to God in their name, humbly beseech him to grant all their petitions; or when they are speaking to them in God's name, pray that the Holy Spirit may fall on all those who hear the word, we should find a more visible good effect of their teaching, and a greater mutual love between ministers and their people.
For ministers' hands would then be held up by the people's intercessions, and the people will never dare to vilify or slander those who are the constant subjects of their prayers.

4. Next to our ministers, our friends claim a place in our intercessions; but then we should not content ourselves with praying for them in general terms, but suit our prayers to their particular circumstances.
When Miriam was afflicted by God with leprosy, Moses cried out and said, "Lord, heal her."
And when the nobleman came to appeal to Jesus Christ on behalf of his child, he said, "Lord, my little daughter is at the point of death; I beg you to come and heal her."
In the same way, when our friends are in any afflicting circumstances, we should endeavor to pray for them with particular regard to those circumstances.
For instance, is a friend sick?

We should pray that, if it is God's good pleasure, it may not lead to death; but if otherwise, that he would give him grace so to bear this visitation that, when this painful life is ended, he may dwell with him in life everlasting.
Is a friend in doubt about an important matter?
We should lay his case before God, as Moses did that of the daughters of Zelophehad, and pray that God's Holy Spirit may lead him into all truth and give him all timely direction.
Is he in need?
We should pray that his faith may never fail, and that in God's due time he may be relieved.

And in all other cases we should not pray for our friends only in general terms, but suit our petitions to their particular sufferings and afflictions; for otherwise we may perhaps never ask for the things our friends most need.

It must be admitted that such a practice will often oblige some to break away from the forms they use; but if we accustom ourselves to it, and have a deep sense of what we are asking for, even the most unlearned will not lack proper words to express themselves.

We have many noble examples in Holy Scripture of the success of this kind of particular intercession, but none more remarkable than that of Abraham's servant in the book of Genesis, who, being sent to seek a wife for his son Isaac, prayed in a most particular manner on his behalf.
And the rest of the story tells us how remarkably his prayer was answered.

And if Christians now prayed for their friends in the same particular manner, and with the same faith, as Abraham's servant did for his master, they would no doubt in many instances receive answers just as visible, and have as much reason to bless God for them as he had. But
5. As we ought thus to intercede for our friends, so in the same way we must also pray for our enemies.
"Bless those who curse you (says Jesus Christ), and pray for those who treat you with spite and persecute you."
This command he enforced in the strongest manner by his own example: in the very agonies and pangs of death he prayed even for his murderers, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do!"

This, it must be admitted, is a difficult duty, yet not impossible for those who have renounced the things of this present life (from an inordinate love of which all enmities arise), and who, knowing the terrible woes pronounced against those who cause Christ's little ones to stumble, can out of real pity and a sense of their danger pray for those through whom such offenses come.

6. Lastly, and to conclude this head, we should intercede for all who are in any way afflicted in mind, body, or circumstances; for all who desire and stand in need of our prayers; and for all who do not pray for themselves.
And oh, that all who hear me would set apart some time every day for the proper performance of this most necessary duty!
To that end,
I shall now proceed,
III. To show the advantages, and to offer some considerations to stir you up to the practice of daily intercession. And
1. First, it will fill your hearts with love for one another.

He who every day heartily intercedes at the throne of grace for all mankind cannot help being filled, in a short time, with love and charity toward all; and the frequent exercise of his love in this manner will imperceptibly enlarge his heart, and make him a partaker of that exceeding abundance of it which is in Christ Jesus our Lord!

Envy, malice, revenge, and similar hellish tempers can never long lodge in a gracious intercessor's breast; but he will be filled with joy, peace, meekness, long-suffering, and all the other graces of the Holy Spirit.
By frequently laying his neighbor's needs before God, he will be touched with a fellow-feeling for them; he will rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep.
Every blessing bestowed on others, instead of stirring up envy in him, will be looked on as an answer to his particular intercession, and will fill his soul with joy inexpressible and full of glory.

Abound, therefore, in acts of general and particular intercession; and when you hear of your neighbor's faults, instead of relating them to others and exposing them before others, lay them in secret before God, and beg him to correct and amend them.

When you hear of a notorious sinner, instead of thinking you do well to be angry, beg Jesus Christ to convert him and make him a monument of his free grace; you cannot imagine what a blessed change this practice will make in your heart, and how much you will grow day by day in the spirit of love and meekness toward all mankind!
But further, to stir you up to the constant practice of this duty of intercession, consider the many examples in Holy Scripture of its power and efficacy.
Great and excellent things are recorded there as the effects of this divine employment.
It has stopped plagues, it has opened and shut heaven, and it has often turned away God's fury from his people.
How was Abimelech's house freed from the disease God sent among them at the intercession of Abraham!
When "Phinehas stood up and prayed," how soon the plague ceased!
When Daniel humbled and afflicted his soul, and interceded for the Lord's inheritance, how quickly an angel was dispatched to tell him "his prayer was heard!"
And, to mention only one more instance, how God acknowledges himself, as it were, overcome by the persistence of Moses when he was interceding for his idolatrous people: "Let me alone," says God!
This sufficiently shows, I could almost say, the omnipotence of intercession, and how we may, like Jacob, wrestle with God, and by a holy violence prevail both for ourselves and for others.

And no doubt it is owing to the secret and prevailing intercessions of the few righteous souls who still remain among us that God has yet spared this miserably sinful nation; for if there were not some such faithful ones left, like Moses, to stand in the gap, we should soon be destroyed, even as Sodom was, and reduced to ashes like Gomorrah.

But to stir you up still further to this exercise of intercession, consider that in all probability it is the frequent employment even of the glorified saints; for though they are delivered from the burden of the flesh, and restored to the glorious liberty of the sons of God, yet since their happiness cannot be perfectly completed until the resurrection of the last day, when all their brothers will be glorified with them, we cannot but think that they are often persistent in beseeching our heavenly Father shortly to complete the number of his elect and to hasten his kingdom.
And shall not we who are on earth often be engaged in this divine employment together with the glorious company of the spirits of just men made perfect?

Since our happiness is to consist so much in the communion of saints in the church triumphant above, shall we not often intercede for the church militant here below, and earnestly beg that we may all be one, even as the holy Jesus and his Father are one, that we also may be made perfect in one?

To provoke you to this great work and labor of love, remember that it is the never-ceasing employment of the holy and highly exalted Jesus himself, who sits at the right hand of God, to hear all our prayers and to make continual intercession for us!
So that he who is constantly employed in interceding for others is doing on earth what the eternal Son of God is always doing in heaven.

Imagine, therefore, when you are lifting up holy hands in prayer for one another, that you see the heavens opened, and the Son of God in all his glory, as the great High Priest of your salvation, pleading for you the all-sufficient merit of his sacrifice before the throne of his heavenly Father!
Join your intercessions, then, with his, and beseech him that through him they may come up as incense, and be received as a sweet fragrance, acceptable in the sight of God!

This picture in your mind will strengthen your faith, stir up a holy earnestness in your prayers, and make you wrestle with God as Jacob did when he saw him face to face and his life was preserved; as Abraham did when he pleaded for Sodom; and as Jesus Christ himself did when, being in agony, he prayed all the more earnestly the night before his bitter passion.
And now, brothers, what more shall I say, since you are taught by Jesus Christ himself to abound in love, and in this good work of praying for one another?
However lowly you may be, though as poor as Lazarus, you will then become benefactors to all mankind; thousands, and twenty times ten thousand, will then be blessed for your sakes!

And after you have spent a few years in this divine exercise here, you will be carried up to that happy place to which you have so often wished others might be raised, and be exalted to sit at the right hand of our All-powerful, All-prevailing Intercessor in the kingdom of his heavenly Father hereafter.

However, I must press this upon you now in a special manner, because all of you among whom I have now been preaching will in all probability see me no more; for I am now going away from you (I trust under the guidance of God's most Holy Spirit), not knowing what will befall me; I therefore need your most persistent intercessions, that nothing may move me from my duty, and that I may not "hold even my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my course with joy, and the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus, to bear witness to the gospel of the grace of God!"

While I have been here, to the best of my knowledge I have not failed to declare to you the whole will of God; and though my preaching may have been a fragrance of death to death to some, yet I trust it has also been a fragrance of life to life to others; and therefore I earnestly hope that these will not fail to remember me in their prayers.

As for me, the many undeserved kindnesses I have received from you will not allow me to forget you; out of the deep, therefore, I trust my cry shall come to God; and while the winds and storms are blowing over me, to the Lord I will make my supplication for you.
For it is only a little while, and "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ," where I must give a strict account of the doctrine I have preached, and you of your improvement under it.
And oh, that I may never be called out as a swift witness against any of those for whose salvation I have sincerely, though too faintly, longed and labored!

It is true that I have been censured by some as acting from sinister and selfish motives; "but with me it is a small matter to be judged by man's judgment." I hope my eye is single; but I beseech you, brothers, by the mercies of God in Christ Jesus, pray that it may be more so!
And that I may grow with the increase of grace in the knowledge and love of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And now, brothers, what more shall I say?
I could wish to continue my discourse much longer, for I can never fully express the desire of my soul toward you!

Finally, therefore, brothers, "whatever things are holy, whatever things are pure, whatever things are honest, whatever things are of good report; if there is any consolation in Christ, if any fellowship of the Spirit," if there is any hope of our appearing to one another's comfort at the awe-inspiring tribunal of Jesus Christ, "think of the things that you have heard," and of those which your pastors have declared and will yet declare to you; and continue under their ministry to "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling," so that whether I never see you again, or whether it pleases God to bring me back at any time, I may always have the satisfaction of knowing that your conduct is such "as befits the gospel of Christ."

I almost persuade myself that I could willingly suffer all things, if it might in any way promote the salvation of your precious and immortal souls; and I beseech you, as my last request, "obey those who have rule over you in the Lord," and always be ready to attend their ministry, as it is your binding duty.

Do not think that I wish to have myself exalted at the expense of another's reputation; but rather think this: not to hold any man's person in too much admiration, but to esteem all your ministers very highly in love, as they justly deserve, for their work's sake.
And now, "brothers, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified."
May God reward you for all your works of faith and labors of love, and make you abound more and more in every good word and work toward all men.
May he truly convert all who have been convicted, and awaken all who are dead in trespasses and sins!
May he establish all who are wavering!

And may you all go on from one degree of grace to another, until you arrive at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and so be made fit to stand before that God "in whose presence is the fullness of joy, and at whose right hand there are pleasures forevermore!" Amen! Amen!

It has been objected by some who dissent from the present ecclesiastical establishment—indeed, I may add, by others also who are actually friends to it—that the ministers of the Church of England preach themselves, and not Christ Jesus the Lord; that they entertain their people with lectures of mere morality, without declaring to them the glad tidings of salvation by Jesus Christ.

How well grounded such an objection may be is not my business to inquire. All I shall say on the point at present is this: whenever such a grave objection is urged against the whole body of the clergy in general, every honest minister of Jesus Christ should do his utmost to cut off every kind of occasion from those who desire an occasion to take offense at us; so that, by hearing us continually sounding forth the word of truth, and declaring with all boldness and assurance of faith “that there is no other name given under heaven by which they can be saved, but that of Jesus Christ,” they may be ashamed of this same confident boasting of theirs against us.

It was a regard for this objection, joined with the pleasantness and delightfulness of the subject (for who can help delighting to speak of that which the blessed angels desire to look into?), that induces me to speak a little on that great and fundamental article of our faith: namely, our being freely justified by the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
“But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the Spirit of our God.”

Since the words begin with the particle “but,” they plainly refer to something that went before; it may therefore not be improper, before I come down to particulars, to consider the words as they stand in relation to the context.

In the verses immediately preceding, the apostle had been listing many notorious sins—drunkenness, adultery, fornication, and the like—the commission of which, without a true and heartfelt repentance, he tells the Corinthians, would entirely shut them out of the kingdom of God.

But then, lest on the one hand they should grow spiritually proud by seeing themselves differ from their unconverted brothers, and so be tempted to despise them and say with the self-conceited hypocrite in the prophet, “Do not come near me, for I am holier than you”; or, on the other hand, by looking back on the multitude of their past offenses, should be inclined to think their sins were too many and too grievous to be forgiven: he first, in order to keep them humble, reminds them of their sad state before conversion, telling them in plain terms, “such (or, as it might be read, these things) were some of you”—not only one, but all that sad catalogue of vices I have been drawing up, some of you were once guilty of; but then, at the same time, to preserve them from despair, see how he brings them glad tidings of great joy: “But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the Spirit of our God.”

The former part of this text, our being sanctified, I have already treated to some extent; I would now enlarge on our being freely justified by the precious obedience and death of Jesus Christ: “But you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
From these words I shall consider three things:
First, what is meant by the word “justified.”
Second, I shall endeavor to prove that all mankind in general, and every individual person in particular, stands in need of being justified.
Third, that there is no possibility of obtaining this justification, which we so greatly need, except by the all-perfect obedience and precious death of Jesus Christ.
First, I am to consider what is meant by the word “justified.”

“But you are justified,” says the apostle; which is as though he had said, You have your sins forgiven, and are regarded by God as though you had never offended him at all: for that is the meaning of the word “justified” in almost all the passages of Holy Scripture where this word is used.

Thus, when this same apostle writes to the Romans, he tells them that “whom God called, those he also justified”; and that this word “justified” implies a blotting out of all our transgressions is evident from what follows, “them he also glorified,” which could not be if a justified person were not regarded by God as though he had never offended him at all.

And again, speaking of Abraham’s faith, he tells them that “Abraham believed on Him who justifies the ungodly”—who acquits and clears the ungodly man; for it is a legal term, and alludes to a judge acquitting an accused criminal of the charge laid against him.
This expression the apostle himself explains by a quotation from the Psalms: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord imputes no sin.”

From all these proofs, and many others that might be offered, it is evident that by being justified we are to understand being so acquitted in the sight of God as to be regarded as though we had never offended him at all.
And in this sense we are to understand that article which we profess to believe in our creed, when each of us declares in his own person, I believe the forgiveness of sins.
This leads me to the
Second thing proposed: to prove that all mankind in general, and every individual person in particular, stands in need of being justified.

And indeed the apostle assumes this in the words of the text, “But you are justified,” thereby implying that the Corinthians (and consequently all mankind, since there is no difference, as will be shown later) stood in need of being justified.

But so as not to rest on bare assumptions, in my further enlargement on this head I shall endeavor to prove that we all stand in need of being justified on account of the sin of our natures and the sin of our lives.
1. First, I affirm that we all stand in need of being justified on account of the sin of our natures: for we are all chargeable with original sin, or the sin of our first parents.

This proposition, though it may be denied by a self-justifying unbeliever who “will not come to Christ that he may have life,” can never be denied by anyone who believes that St. Paul’s epistles were written by divine inspiration; for there we are told that “in Adam all died”—that is, Adam’s sin was imputed to all; and lest we should forget to make a particular application, it is added in another place “that there is none who does good (that is, by nature), no, not one; that we have all gone out of the way (of original righteousness), and are by nature the children of wrath.”

And even David, who was a man after God’s own heart, and who, if anyone could, might surely plead an exemption from this universal corruption, yet confesses that “he was shaped in iniquity, and that in sin his mother conceived him.”

And, to mention only one more text, as immediately applicable to the present purpose, St. Paul, in his epistle to the Romans, says that “Death came upon all men through the disobedience of one, namely, of Adam, even upon those (that is, little children) who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam’s transgression”; who had not been guilty of actual sin, and therefore could not have been punished with temporal death (which came into the world, as this same apostle tells us elsewhere, only by sin) had not the disobedience of our first parents been imputed to them.

So what has been said on this point seems to be excellently summed up in that article of our church where she declares that “Original sin does not stand in the following of Adam, but it is the fault and corruption of every man that is naturally engendered of the offspring of Adam; whereby man is very far gone from original righteousness, and is of his own nature inclined to evil, so that the flesh always desires what is contrary to the spirit; and therefore in every person born into this world it deserves God’s wrath and damnation.”

I have been more detailed in treating this point because it is the very foundation of the Christian religion: for I am truly persuaded that it is nothing but a lack of being well grounded in the doctrine of original sin, and of the helpless—indeed, I may say, damnable—condition in which each of us comes into the world, that makes so many unbelievers oppose, and so many who call themselves Christians so very lukewarm in their love and affection toward Jesus Christ.
It is this, and I could almost say this alone, that makes unbelief abound among us as much as it does.

For, alas, we are mistaken if we imagine that men now become or remain unbelievers, and set up corrupted reason in opposition to divine revelation, merely for lack of evidence (for I believe it might easily be proved that a modern unbeliever is the most credulous creature living); no, it is only the lack of a humble mind, of a sense of their original depravity, and of a willingness to acknowledge themselves so depraved, that makes them so obstinately shut their eyes against the light of the glorious gospel of Christ.

Whereas, on the contrary, if they were but once cut to the heart with a due and lively sense of their natural corruption and liability to condemnation, we would no longer have them scoffing at divine revelation and regarding it as an idle tale; but they would cry out with the trembling jailer, “What shall I do to be saved?”
It was an error on this fundamental point that made so many resist the evidence which the Son of God himself gave of his divine mission when he dwelt among us.
Every word he spoke, every action he did, every miracle he worked, proved that he came from God.
Why then did so many harden their hearts and refuse to believe his report?

Why, he himself tells us: “They will not come to me that they may have life.” They will obstinately hold out against the means God had appointed for their salvation. And St. Paul tells us “that if the gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who are lost, in whom the god of this world has blinded the eyes of those who do not believe, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine on them.”
If it is asked, how does it agree with the divine goodness to impute the guilt of one man’s sin to an innocent posterity?
I should think it sufficient to use the apostle’s words: “No, but, O man, who are you to reply against God?
Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me like this?”

But to give a more direct reply: people would do well to consider that in the first covenant God made with man, Adam acted as a public person, as the common representative of all mankind, and consequently we must stand or fall with him.

Had he continued in his obedience and not eaten the forbidden fruit, the benefits of that obedience would doubtless have been imputed to us; but since he did not persist in it, but broke the covenant made with him, and with us in him, who dares charge the righteous Judge of all the earth with injustice for imputing that to us also? I proceed,
Second, to prove that we stand in need of being justified on account of the sin of our lives.

That God, since he made man, has a right to demand his obedience is, I suppose, a truth no one will deny; that he has also given us both a natural and a written law, by which we are to be judged, cannot be questioned by anyone who believes St. Paul’s epistle to the Romans to be of divine authority: for in it we are told of a law written in the heart, and a law given by Moses; and that each of us has broken these laws is all too evident from our sad and frequent experience.
Accordingly, the Holy Scriptures tell us that “there is no man who lives and does not sin”; that “in many things we all offend”; that “if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”; and the like.

And if we are thus offenders against God, it follows that we stand in need of forgiveness for so offending him—unless we suppose that God enacts laws and at the same time does not care whether they are obeyed or not; which is as absurd as to suppose that a prince should establish laws for the proper government of his country, and yet let every violator of them go unpunished.

But God has not dealt so foolishly with his creatures. No, as he gave us a law, he demands our obedience to that law, and has bound us to obey it universally and perseveringly, under no lesser penalty than incurring his curse and eternal death for every breach of it; for thus the Scripture speaks: “Cursed is he who does not continue in all things that are written in the law, to do them”; as the Scripture also says in another place, “The soul who sins, it shall die.”
Now it has already been proved that we have all sinned; and therefore, unless some means can be found to satisfy God’s justice, we must perish eternally.
Let us then stand still a while, and see in what a deplorable condition each of us comes into the world, and continues, until we are transferred into a state of grace.

For surely nothing more deplorable can well be imagined than to be born under the curse of God; to be charged with original guilt; and not only so, but to be convicted as actual breakers of God’s law, the least breach of which justly deserves eternal damnation.
Surely this can be only a melancholy prospect in which to view ourselves, and it must set us to devising some means by which we may satisfy and appease our offended Judge.
But what must those means be?
Shall we repent? Alas! there is not one word of repentance mentioned in the first covenant: “The day that you eat of it, you shall surely die.”
So that, if God is true, unless some way is found to satisfy divine justice, we must perish; and there is no room left for us to expect a change of mind in God, though we should seek it with tears.
Well then, if repentance will not do, shall we plead the law of works?
Alas! “By the law no man living shall be justified: for by the law comes the knowledge of sin.”
It is the law that convicts and condemns, and therefore it can by no means justify us; and “all our righteousnesses (says the prophet) are only like filthy rags.”
With what then shall we come before the Lord, and bow down before the most high God?
Shall we come before him with calves a year old, with thousands of rams, or ten thousands of rivers of oil?

Alas! God has shown you, O man, that this will not avail; for he has declared, “I will take no bull out of your house, nor male goat out of your fold: for all the beasts of the forests are mine, and so are the cattle on a thousand hills.”
Will the Lord then be pleased to accept our firstborn for our transgression, the fruit of our bodies for the sin of our souls?
Even this will not purchase our pardon, for he has declared that “the children shall not bear the iniquities of their parents.”
Besides, they are sinners, and therefore, being under the same condemnation, they stand in need of forgiveness just as much as we do.
They are impure; and will the Lord accept the blind and the lame for sacrifice?
Shall some angel then, or archangel, undertake to fulfill the covenant which we have broken, and make atonement for us?

Alas! they are only creatures, though creatures of the highest order; and therefore they are obliged to obey God as well as we are; and after they have done all, they must say they have done no more than what was their duty to do.
And supposing it were possible for them to die, yet how could the death of a finite creature satisfy an infinitely offended justice?
O wretched men that we are!
Who shall deliver us?
I thank God, our Lord Jesus Christ.
This naturally leads me to the

Third thing proposed, which was to endeavor to prove that there is no possibility of obtaining this justification, which we so greatly need, except by the all-perfect obedience and precious death of Jesus Christ: “But you are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

But since this has been proved to some extent by what was said under the previous head, where I have shown that neither our repentance, righteousness, nor sacrifice—no, not even the obedience and death of angels themselves—could possibly procure justification for us, nothing remains for me to do under this head but to show that Jesus Christ has procured it for us.
And here I shall still turn “to the law and to the testimony.”

For after all the most subtle disputes on either side, nothing but the living oracles of God can give us any satisfaction on this momentous point, it being such an inconceivable mystery that the eternal, only begotten Son of God should die for sinful man, that we would not have dared so much as to think of it, had not God revealed it in his holy word.
It is true, reason may show us the wound, but only revelation can lead us to the means of our cure.

And though the method God has been pleased to take to make us happy may be a stumbling block to the unbeliever, and foolishness to the opinionated wise man and disputer of this world, yet wisdom—that is, the dispensation of our redemption—will be justified, approved, and submitted to by all her truly wise and holy children, by every sincere and upright Christian.
But to come more directly to the point before us.
Two things, as was observed before, we needed in order to be at peace with God:
1. To be freed from the guilt of the sin of our nature.
2. From the sin of our lives.
And both of these (thanks be to God for this unspeakable gift) are secured to believers by the obedience and death of Jesus Christ.
For what does the Scripture say?

1. As to the first, it tells us that “as by the disobedience of one man (or by one transgression, namely, that of Adam) many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one, Jesus Christ (therein including his passive as well as his active obedience), many were made righteous.”

And again, “As by the disobedience of one man judgment came upon all men to condemnation”—that is, all men were condemned by having Adam’s sin imputed to them—“so by the obedience of one, that is, Jesus Christ, the free gift of pardon and peace came upon all men (all sorts of men) to justification of life.”

I say all sorts of men; for the apostle in this chapter is only drawing a parallel between the first and the second Adam in this respect, that they both acted as representatives; and as the posterity of Adam had his sin imputed to them, so those for whom Christ died, and whose representative he is, shall have his merits imputed to them also.

Whoever runs the parallel further in order to prove universal redemption (whatever arguments they may draw for the proof of it from other passages of Scripture)—if they would draw one from this passage for that purpose, I think they stretch their line of interpretation beyond the limits of Scripture.
2. Pardon for the sin of our lives was another thing which we needed to have secured to us before we could be at peace with God.
And this, the Holy Scriptures tell us, is abundantly done by the death of Jesus Christ.

The evangelical prophet foretold that the promised Redeemer would be “wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our iniquities; that the chastisement of our peace would be upon him; and that by his stripes we would be healed,” Isaiah 53:6.
The angels at his birth said that he would “save his people from their sins.”
And St. Paul declares that “this is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.”

And here in the words of the text: “Such (or, as I observed before, these things) were some of you; but you are washed, etc.” And again: “Jesus Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

And to show us that none but Jesus Christ can do all this, the apostle St. Peter says, “Nor is there salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, but the name of Jesus Christ.”
How God will be pleased to deal with the Gentiles, who still sit in darkness and under the shadow of death, and on whom the sun of righteousness has never yet risen, is not for us to inquire.
“What have we to do with judging those who are outside?”

To God’s mercy let us commend them, and wait for the solution of this and every other difficult point until the great day of accounts, when all God’s dispensations, both of providence and of grace, will be fully cleared up by methods as yet unknown to us, because unrevealed.
However, this we know: that the Judge of all the earth will most assuredly do right.
But it is time for me to draw to a conclusion.
I have now, brothers, by the blessing of God, spoken on the words of the text in the method I proposed.

Many useful inferences might be drawn from what has been delivered; but since I have detained you, I fear, too long already, permit me only to make a reflection or two on what has been said, and I am done.

If, then, we are freely justified by the death and obedience of Jesus Christ, let us pause here a while; and as we have already reflected on the misery of a fallen soul, let us now turn aside and see the happiness of the believing soul.

But alas! how lost I am in the thought that God the Father, when we were in a state of enmity and rebellion against him, should nevertheless yearn in his heart toward us, his fallen, his apostate creatures; and, because nothing but an infinite ransom could satisfy an infinitely offended justice, should send his only and dear Son Jesus Christ (who is God, blessed forever, and who had lain in his bosom from all eternity) to fulfill the covenant of works, and to die a cursed, painful, shameful death for us and for our salvation! Who can keep from crying out at the consideration of this mystery of godliness?
“Oh, the depth of the riches of God’s love” to us, his wretched, miserable, and undone creatures!
“How unsearchable is his mercy, and his ways past finding out!”
Now we know in truth, O God, that you have loved us, “since you have not withheld your Son, your only Son Jesus Christ,” from thus doing and dying for us.
But as we admire the Father in sending, let us likewise humbly and thankfully adore the Son in coming, when sent to die for man.

But oh! what thoughts can conceive, what words express, the infinite greatness of that unparalleled love which moved the Son of God to come down from the mansions of his Father’s glory to obey and die for sinful man!
The Jews, when he merely shed a tear at poor Lazarus’ funeral, said, “See how he loved him.”
How much more justly, then, may we cry out, See how he loved us!
When he not only fulfilled the whole moral law, but did not spare to shed his own most precious blood for us.
And can any poor, truly convicted sinner despair of mercy after this?
What, can they see their Savior hanging on a tree, with arms stretched out ready to embrace them, and yet, when they truly believe in him, doubt of finding acceptance with him?
No, away with all such dishonoring, despairing thoughts.
