Look at his hands, bored through with pins of iron; look at his side, pierced with a cruel spear to let loose the floodgates of his blood and open a fountain for sin and for all uncleanness; and then despair of mercy if you can!

No, only believe in him, and then, though you have crucified him afresh, he will abundantly pardon you: “though your sins are as scarlet, yet they shall be as wool; though deeper than crimson, yet they shall be whiter than snow.”
Which may God of his infinite mercy grant, etc.

This psalm is called the song of loves—the most pure and spiritual, the most dear and delightful loves; namely, those which are between Christ the beloved and his church, which is his spouse. In it is set forth, first, the Lord Jesus Christ with regard to his majesty, power, and divinity, his truth, meekness, and equity; and then the spouse is set forth with regard to her ornaments, companions, attendants, and posterity; and both with regard to their comeliness and beauty.

After the description of Christ, an invitation to his espousals is given to the children of men, who are called by the name of daughter; and therefore it applies particularly to you, my dear sisters, since you are the daughters of men—yet not so as to exclude the sons of men.
I shall now, therefore, consider the words as spoken to you in particular, and as containing this doctrine:

That the Lord Jesus Christ invites the daughters of men to be his spouse, and greatly desires the beauty of those who, forgetting their own people and their father’s house, listen, consider, and incline to his invitation, and join themselves to him in this relation.
I shall show:
I. How Christ espouses himself to the children of men, but more especially to the daughters of men.

The Lord Jesus Christ espouses himself to the children of men in this world, but the public solemnization of the marriage is reserved until the last day, when his spouse shall be brought forth to him in white robes and a garment of perfect righteousness, richer and more exquisite, my dear sisters, than any of your needlework; and the marriage feast will be kept in his Father’s house in heaven, when they shall be received into the nearest and closest embraces of his love.
The marriage knot is tied here, and in it four things are included:
First, mutual choice;
Secondly, mutual affection;
Thirdly, mutual union;
Fourthly, mutual obligation.

First, my dear sisters, there is a mutual choice, which is not only in Christ as Mediator, but also by Christ as the eternal Son of God—yes, God himself—notwithstanding all that the polite Arians and Socinians say to the contrary.

The Lord Jesus Christ, my dear sisters, chooses you purely by his free grace; it is freely of his own mercy that he brings you into the marriage covenant. You who have so grievously offended him—yet the Lord Jesus Christ has chosen you. You did not, you would not, have chosen him; but once he has chosen you, my dear sisters, then, and not until then, you make choice of him as your Lord and Husband.

When the Lord Jesus Christ first comes to you, he finds you full of sin and pollution; you are deformed, defiled, enslaved, poor, miserable, and wretched, very despicable and loathsome because of sin. And he chooses you, not because of your holiness, nor your beauty, nor because you are qualified for them; no, the Lord Jesus Christ puts such qualifications upon you as may make you fit for his embrace; and you are drawn to choose the Lord Jesus Christ because he first chose you.
Secondly, in this espousal of yours, my dear sisters, there is a mutual affection; this accompanies the choice.

Your hearts are drawn out after Christ; your souls pant and long for him; you cannot rest until you are engaged to this Jesus. You are ready to cry out continually, “None but Christ, none but Christ!” This is the language of your hearts, if you are truly aware of your need of him.
The better acquainted you become with this Lord Jesus, the more pleased you are with your choice, and the more your affections are drawn toward him.
And where can you place your affections better than upon that Jesus who shed his blood for your sakes?
Surely he deserves both your love and your affections. Go on, go on, my dear sisters, so that your affections may grow stronger and stronger.

Thirdly, there is not only mutual choice and mutual affection, but also mutual union; and here the marriage chiefly lies, in this union. Christ and souls are contracted, and the knot is tied so fast that neither men on earth, however great they may be, nor devils in hell, even if they should combine all their wrath and rage together, can dissolve it or untie it. No, my dear sisters, it is indissoluble, for the union is by the Spirit on Christ’s part, and by faith on yours. By the Spirit Christ lays hold on you, and by faith you lay hold on him; and so the match is made. Christ becomes yours—his person, his portion, and all his benefits are yours; and you become Christ’s—your persons, your hearts, and all that you have are surrendered to him. And O that they may be so more and more!
Fourthly, there is a mutual obligation between Christ and his spouse.

Christ binds himself to love you here; he will not—indeed, he never will—leave you. He will protect you from the malice of the Pharisees of this generation; he will provide for you in all difficulties; he will live with you here, and at last he will take you to himself, to live with him forever.

And you are bound to him to be loving, loyal, faithful, and obedient; and you are to cling closely to him as long as you live. And then you will find that you have married to the best advantage, both for soul and body, for time and for eternity.
II. Christ invites all of you to be his spouse.
And it is for this reason that he sends forth his ministers to preach.
It is this that makes me come among you in this way: that you would accept this invitation, to which I call you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and entreat you to take him on his own terms.

He calls all of you, my sisters, whether older or younger, married or unmarried, of high rank or of the lowest station, the poorest servants—yes, the rabble of this world, as the world calls you—who are willing to be espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ.
I say, the poor are as welcome to be Christ’s spouse as those who are rich.

He does not regard the rich more than the poor; he chose a humble virgin, engaged to a carpenter, to be his mother; and he chooses and calls all such to be his spouse. So do not be discouraged that you are despised in the world; for if you are only loved by Christ and espoused to him, it will more than make up for all the trouble you have met with here.
III. Those who would be espoused to Christ must listen, consider, and incline to his invitation, and forget even their father’s house.
Those who would be espoused to Christ must listen.

“Listen, O daughter.” Many among you, my sisters, stop their ears against the calls of the gospel; they shut their ears like the deaf adder, which will not listen to the voice of the charmer, however wisely he charms.

You will not listen to the invitations of Christ; you can listen to the vanities of the world and be delighted with the espousals of the world, but you never think of, nor are delighted with, the espousals of Christ.

It was by the ear that the temptation of sin was received by the first man, when he departed from God; and by the ear the invitation to be Christ’s spouse must be received, before the heart will be opened to receive Jesus Christ in this marriage relation.
If you would be espoused to Christ, my dear sisters, you must consider Christ’s invitation.

It is not a careless or mere hearing of Christ’s invitation that will be of any use to you, or will make up the match between Christ and your souls; no, you must receive Christ in the heart. You must consider the thing itself, its advantages, and the difference between Christ’s invitations and the devil’s temptations, or any of the world’s offers.
Those who would be espoused to Christ must be inclined to accept Christ’s invitation.
“Listen, O daughter, consider, and incline your ear.”

This means to incline your hearts. You must consent with your wills; there must be compliance with the proposal of Christ, and you must have desires after Christ; and then your hearts will say, “Lord, let us be your spouse, and may you be our beloved.”
You must also forget your father’s house.
“Listen, O daughter, and consider, and forget your father’s house.”

You are not here told to cast off all affection for your natural relations; but you must forget all relations to the extent of being ready to give up all their favor, when it stands in competition with that of the Lord Jesus Christ. And do not let your worldly friends and relations hinder you from closing with and espousing the Lord Jesus.

I earnestly beg you to suffer the loss of anything rather than lose his favors. You must indeed forget your own people; that is, you must forget all the evil customs you have learned in your father’s house, and forsake all your vain conduct—your reading of plays, novels, or romances; and you must keep from learning to sing the songs of the drunkard; for Christ, if you are his spouse, has redeemed you.
Those of you, my dear sisters, who are espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ are very beautiful.

I do not mean with respect to your bodies; you may have less outward comeliness than others as far as your bodies are concerned, but as to your souls you will excel in beauty—not so much in the eyes of man as in the eyes of God. Such people have the most beautiful image of God stamped upon them; no one else in the world has the least spark of spiritual beauty.
Those who are not married to Christ are unregenerate; they are not born again, nor brought from sin to God, which must be done before you are espoused to Christ.

And the Lord Jesus Christ desires to see this beauty in his spouse, for he cries out, “O my dove, you are in the clefts of the rock, in the hidden places of the stairs; let me see your countenance, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is comely.”
He calls his spouse his love, since she is the dear object of his love; and he admires her loveliness. He repeats it twice in one verse: “See, you are fair, my love; see, you are fair.”
So you see how he describes their beauty.

And then, my sisters, we have a wonderful expression of Christ to his spouse: “You have captivated my heart, my sister, my spouse; you have captivated my heart with one of your eyes, with one chain of your neck.”
So you see how pleased the Lord Jesus Christ is with his spouse; and will you not, therefore, be espoused to the Lord Jesus?
I offer Jesus Christ to all of you. However notorious you have been for sin—even if you have been as great a harlot as Mary Magdalene was—once you are espoused to Christ, you shall be forgiven.

Therefore do not be discouraged by whatever slights and contempt the world may heap upon you, but come and join yourselves to the Lord Jesus Christ, and all your sins shall be washed away in his blood. And once you are espoused to Jesus, you are separated from sin; you are born again.

You are now, as it were, espoused to sin; sin is your husband, and you are too fond of it. But once you are married to Christ, when you are born again, then you may be said to die to sin; but until then, sin lives in your affections. Therefore, my sisters, give sin its death-wound in your hearts. You have been called by the word time after time, and it has had no effect on you; but when you are espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ, then you will be brought to him by his Spirit. You will then lay hold on him by faith; his Spirit will draw you to himself; he will make you willing in the day of his power; he will give you faith in him.

Faith is the hand of the soul which lays hold on Christ; therefore do not rest content until you have this grace of faith worked in you with power; do not be content until you have received the Lord Jesus Christ.

Embrace Christ in the arms of your dearest love. You love the Lord Jesus Christ with sincerity when you love and esteem him above father, mother, and all the delights and pleasures of this life; but if you delight in anything this world can produce more than in the Lord Jesus Christ, you do not have true love for him.

If you are espoused to Christ, you have acquaintance and fellowship with him; you will endeavor to promote his interest and advance his name in the world. When others are going to the polite and fashionable amusements of life, you will be laboring to bring honor to the Lord Jesus Christ; you will commend your beloved above all other beloveds, and endeavor to bring others to love him.
Can you, my dear sisters, who are now assembled to worship God, show such evidence of your espousals to the Lord Jesus Christ?
O how joyful, how comforting a state this is!
Surely this is a marriage worth seeking after; this is the only desirable marriage, and the Lord Jesus Christ is the only lover worth seeking after.
Now, my dear sisters, I shall speak a few words to those of you who have not yet espoused yourselves to the Lord Jesus.
It is a great sin, and surely you greatly affront the Lord who bought you.

It is also your folly to refuse and neglect the gracious offers of being the spouse of Christ. By this you forfeit all the love he would bestow on you; by this you choose rags before robes, dross before gold, pebbles before jewels, guilt before a pardon, wounds before healing, defilement before cleansing, deformity before comeliness, trouble before peace, slavery before liberty, the service of the devil before the service of Christ.
By this you choose dishonor before a crown, death before life, hell before heaven, eternal misery and torment before everlasting joy and glory.
And is there need of any further evidence of your folly and madness in refusing and neglecting Christ as your spouse?
My dear sisters, I would exceed the limits of your time if I were to set out in detail all the advantages you would obtain by being espoused to the Lord Jesus.

This is your wisdom: they are foolish virgins who refuse; but you are the wise virgins who have accepted the Lord Jesus Christ and have given yourselves to him. You have made the wisest choice; and however the blind world may consider you fools, and despise you as being methodically mad, yet you are wise in the esteem of God, and will one day appear so in the esteem of those who now despise you.

It is your glory that you are espoused to the Lord Jesus; and therefore glory in your espousal—glory not in yourselves, but in the Lord who has so freely and graciously bestowed these favors upon you.

It is your safety to be espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ; he will protect and defend you even from sin and Satan and eternal ruin, and so far you are safe. He has regard for you in times of danger from men, and these times of danger seem to be hastening on. It is now rising like a black cloud no bigger than a man’s hand, and by and by it will spread over the heavens, and when it is full it will burst; but if you are espoused to Christ, you are safe.
Now, my dear sisters, I shall conclude with an earnest exhortation to high and low, rich and poor, one with another, to be espoused to Christ.
Let me speak in a special way to you young women who are not yet espoused to Christ.
It may be that a wish to satisfy your curiosity has brought many of you here; yet perhaps this may be the time when you shall be brought home to embrace the Lord Jesus and be espoused to him.
And O that I may persuade you, by his Spirit, to espouse yourselves to the Lord of life!
And if you are only brought to close with the Lord Jesus Christ, I shall attain my end, and then both you and I shall rejoice that I preached this sermon to you.
Come, virgins, will you give me permission to be a suitor to you—not in my own name, but in the name of the Lord?
O that I may prevail with you for your affections, and persuade you to give them to Christ!
May I be the instrument of bringing your souls to Christ!
May I be the instrument of joining you and Christ together this day!

Do not be coy (bashful, shy; showing reluctance to make a definite commitment), as some of you perhaps are in other loves. Modesty and the virgin blush may very well become you when proposals of another kind are made to you; but here coyness is silly, and backwardness to accept this proposal is shameful. You have ten thousand times more reason to blush at refusing Christ as your beloved than at accepting him—when otherwise the devil and sin would carry off your virgin affections.
Never was a better proposal made to you; never was such a match offered to you as this—of being matched and espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Consider who the Lord Jesus is, to whom you are invited to espouse yourselves: he is the best husband; there is none comparable to Jesus Christ.
Do you desire one who is great?
He is of the highest dignity; he is the glory of heaven, the darling of eternity, admired by angels, dreaded by devils, and adored by saints.
For you to be espoused to so great a king—what honor will you have by this espousal?
Do you desire one who is rich?
None is comparable to Christ; the fullness of the earth belongs to him.

If you are espoused to Christ, you shall share in his unsearchable riches; you shall receive of his fullness, even grace for grace, here, and hereafter you shall be admitted to glory, and shall live with this Jesus for all eternity.
Do you desire one who is wise?
There is none comparable to Christ for wisdom.
His knowledge is infinite, and his wisdom corresponds to it.
And if you are espoused to Christ, he will guide and counsel you, and make you wise for salvation.
Do you desire one who is mighty, who can defend you against your enemies, and against all the insults and reproaches of the Pharisees of this generation?
There is none who can equal Christ in power; for the Lord Jesus Christ has all power.
Do you desire one who is good?
There is none like Christ in this respect; others may have some goodness, but it is imperfect. Christ’s goodness is complete and perfect; he is full of goodness, and in him dwells no evil.
Do you desire one who is beautiful?
His eyes are most sparkling, his looks and glances of love are enrapturing, his smiles are most delightful and refreshing to the soul: Christ is the loveliest person of all in the world.
Do you desire one who can love you?

None can love you like Christ. His love, my dear sisters, is incomprehensible; his love surpasses all other loves. The love of the Lord Jesus is first, without beginning; his love is free, without any motive; his love is great, without any measure; his love is constant, without any change; and his love is everlasting.

It was the love of the Lord Jesus Christ, my dear sisters, which brought him down from heaven, and which veiled his divinity in a human soul and body; for he is God over all, blessed forever. It was love that made him subject to hunger, thirst, and sorrow; he was humbled even to death for you. For you who are espoused to him he underwent the painful, shameful, and ignominious death of the cross. And can you, my sisters, hear this and not be moved to think that the blessed Jesus underwent all this for such sinful creatures as you and I are?

And when, out of love, he had finished the redemption on earth, as far as was needed for satisfaction, it was his love that carried him back to heaven, where he was before, so that he might apply what he had purchased, that there he might make intercession for those whom he had redeemed, and prepare a place for them—even glorious mansions with himself, in the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
It is out of love that he sends such tokens to his people from heaven to earth, which he conveys to them through his ordinances, by his Spirit.

Surely, then, none is so deserving as the Lord Jesus Christ for you to espouse yourselves to. If you are espoused to Christ, he is yours—all that he is and all that he has; you shall have his heart, and share in the choicest expressions of his dearest love.
The Lord Jesus Christ, my dear sisters, begs you to be his spouse.
We ministers have a commission from the Lord Jesus Christ to invite you, in his name, to this very thing; and Christ’s invitations are real, general, frequent, earnest, and free.
Christ’s invitations to you to be his spouse are real; and as the thing is real, so you, my dear sisters, are really invited to it.

The Lord does not mock and deceive you, like some pretending lovers who feign love to virgins until they have gained their affections, and then falsely and basely abandon them, never really intending either to espouse or to marry them. But the Lord really intends the thing in his invitations to you; he never cast off anyone whose consent and affections he had gained. Again,
Christ’s invitations to you, my dear sisters, are general.

All of you are invited; none of you are excluded. All sorts of sinners are invited; the most vile and abominable sinners, the most notorious transgressors, are invited to be Christ’s spouse, and shall be as welcome as any to the embraces of his love.

Christ’s invitations to you are frequent. Jesus Christ calls on you frequently; he has waited on you time after time, one year after another; and he now invites you, through me, this day, to come to him.
Do not slight this invitation, but receive it with joy and thankfulness.
Come, I beg you, to this Jesus, who thus invites you to be his spouse. Again,

Christ’s invitations to be his spouse are earnest. He calls upon you—and not only calls, but calls earnestly too; yes, he uses many arguments with you; he will press you to come to him; he is unwilling to take any denial from you. He knocks, and knocks hard, at the door of your hearts to be received; and surely you will not deny the Lord of life and glory, who died for you and gave himself for you. O my dear sisters, let this be the evening of your espousals to the Lord Jesus Christ.

He invites you freely to be his spouse, for all his invitations are free; he does not expect a dowry with you, as worldly lovers do. He wants nothing from you; no, you must have nothing, if you would be espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ.

If you are poor, miserable, blind, and naked, Jesus Christ will supply all these defects out of his own free mercy; he will fill and supply you with all things out of his treasury; he will make you fit for himself; he will prepare you to live with him forever.

Consider: if you are once espoused to Christ, once joined in this relation, you shall never be separated from him; neither men nor devils shall be able to separate you. None—none—shall part you; and when death breaks all other bonds, it shall not break the marriage bond between you and Christ, but shall bring you into the most full and everlasting possession of your beloved.
And what do you now say, young women?

Shall I have consent for my master, or be sent away with a rebuff and refusal? No, I cannot carry such a message to my master; I hope better things of you, my sisters, and things that accompany salvation. It seems to me that by this time you should begin to have a mind for Jesus Christ; you look as if you desired him; you listen as if you would consent.
What do you say?
Shall the match be made this evening between Christ and your souls?
O that I may be the instrument of joining your hands—or rather your hearts—together! O that I may be the instrument to tie that knot which can never be loosed!

Some marry in haste and repent at leisure; but if you were once espoused to Jesus Christ, you would never repent. Nothing would grieve you except that you were not joined to him sooner; and you would not be separated again for all the world.
Shall this be the day of your espousals?
Some of you have waited a long time; and will you delay any longer?

If you will not now, perhaps you may never have another opportunity; this may be the last time of asking, and therefore it is dangerous to refuse. Some of you are very young, too young for other espousals; but none of you, my dear sisters, are too young to be espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ. In other espousals you must have the consent of your parents; but in this you are at your own disposal. You may give yourselves, and ought to match yourselves, to Christ, whether your parents consent or not.
But what if any of you should ask what you must do in order to be espoused to Christ?

You must be aware of your need of being espoused to him, and until you are aware of your need of the Lord Jesus Christ, you cannot be espoused to him. You must have desires after this Jesus, and seek him for an interest in him; you must cry to him nightly to espouse you to himself. Put off the filthiness of sin and all its defilements; and then, my sisters, put on the white raiment and clean garments which Christ has provided for you, the robes of his righteousness. In these garments you shall be beautiful, and in these garments you shall be accepted. You must have the wedding garment on; you must put off all your own good works, for they will only be a means of keeping you from Christ. No, you must come as not having your own righteousness, which is of the law, but you must have the righteousness of Christ.
Therefore, come to the Lord Jesus Christ, and he will give it to you; he will not send you away without it.

Receive him on his own terms, and he is yours forever. O devote yourselves to him, soul and body and all, to be his forever; and Christ will be yours—and then happy, happy are you that you were ever born!

But if any of you die before this espousal to the Lord Jesus Christ, then woe, woe to you that you ever had a being in life! But if you go to Christ, you shall be espoused to the Lord Jesus. However great your sins have been, yes, the blood of Christ will cleanse you from them; the marriage covenant between Christ and your souls will dissolve all your sins. You will then be weary of your old ways, for all things will become new in your souls.
Now, my dear sisters, I shall conclude by speaking just a word or two to those of you who are already espoused to the Lord Jesus Christ.
O admire, admire the rich and free grace which has brought you into this relation! Is not this an instance of the greatest love, that you should be the spouse of the Lord Jesus Christ?
You who had no beauty, you who had no comeliness, who were full of sin—that he should embrace such as you and I are; that we should be taken into the embrace of this Lord Jesus!
O infinite, condescending kindness!
O amazing love! Reverence, reverence this Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you.

He is your Lord, and you must reverence him, love him, and be faithful to him, be subject to him, and be careful to please him in everything. Endeavor to keep up a daily communion with him; look for, long for, and prepare for Christ’s second appearing, when the nuptials between you shall be solemnized, and you shall live with him in mansions of everlasting joy, where you shall love and live with this King of glory forever and ever.

I do not know how to conclude; it seems to me I could speak to you until midnight, if it would bring you to the Lord Jesus Christ and cause you to be espoused to him. For indeed that will be the espousal that will turn to the greatest advantage, as you will find by experience, if you will only make the trial; and that you may do so, my prayers and my constant endeavor shall be employed.

I will, my dear sisters, spend and be spent for you, and by the help of God I will persevere in this that I have begun. And since many of you may have opportunity some evening in the week, without interfering with the business of life, I shall therefore, my sisters, be either here or wherever you shall be publicly informed. I will not mind being reproached or despised; the men of this world may use whatever language they please; they may say I am a Methodist.

Indeed, my sisters, I am resolved, by the grace of God, to use all the methods I can to pluck you from Satan, that you may be as brands plucked from the burning fire. This shall be my method, which I hope will be the means of effectually saving your precious and immortal souls.

And if I am the instrument of this, I shall rejoice—yes, and I will rejoice—in spite of whatever men or devils can say or do to the contrary. And may the Lord Jesus Christ direct and assist me at all times to do what will be most for his glory and the welfare of your souls; and may you all say a hearty Amen to it.

“Now may the Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever, assist and watch over you, keep you from all evil and sin here, and present you faultless before his Father at the great day of account!

To this Lord Jesus Christ, the Father, and the blessed Spirit, three persons and yet but one eternal and invisible God, be ascribed all honor, power, glory, might, majesty, and dominion, now, henceforth, and forevermore. Amen, Amen.”

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all, to comfort you under tribulation and deliver you from it; to preserve you to your respective places of abode; and when you are there, to keep you in his fear, that you may live to his glory; that to live may be Christ, and to die be your eternal gain; so that you may live with him through eternal ages, and sing Hallelujahs to him forever. Amen.”
1 Corinthians 13:8 — “Charity never fails.”
Nothing is more valuable and commendable, and yet no duty is less practiced, than that of charity.

We often pretend concern and pity for the misery and distress of our fellow creatures, yet we seldom sympathize with their condition enough to relieve them according to our abilities; but unless we assist them with what they may need, for the body as well as for the soul, all our wishes are no more than words of no value or regard, and are not to be esteemed or regarded: for when we hear of any deplorable circumstance in which our fellow creatures are involved, whether they are friends or enemies, it is our duty as Christians to assist them to the utmost of our power.

Indeed, my brethren, we are not to hurt ourselves or our families; this is not the charity that is so highly recommended by St. Paul; no, but if we are in any way able to relieve them without injuring either ourselves or our families, then it is our duty to do it; and this never fails, where it proceeds from a right end and with a right view.

St. Paul had been showing, in the preceding chapter, that spiritual gifts were diverse; that God had allotted one blessing to one and another to another; and though there was a diversity of blessings, God did not bestow them on one person, but gave to one a blessing which he denied to another, and gave a blessing or a gift to the other which might make him as eminent in one way as the other's gift made him in another: but though there are these diverse spiritual gifts, they are all given for some wise end, namely, for the profit of all, and to that end they are bestowed in these different ways.

We are not, on the one hand, to hide those gifts which God has given us; nor are we, on the other, to be so lavish with them as to spend them on our lusts and pleasures, to satisfy our sensual appetites; but they are to be used for the glory of God and the good of immortal souls.

After he had illustrated this in detail, he goes on to show that all gifts, however great they may be in themselves, are of no value unless we have charity, as you may see particularly by considering this chapter from the beginning.

But before I go any further, I shall tell you what the apostle means by charity; and that is, love; if there is true love, there will be charity; there will be an effort to assist, help, and relieve according to the ability with which God has blessed us: and since this is so highly recommended by the apostle, let us see how valuable this charity is, and how commendable in all those who pursue it. I shall,
I. Consider this blessing as it relates to the bodies of men.
II. I shall show how much more valuable it is when it relates to the souls of men.
III. I shall show you when your charity is of the right kind.
IV. Why this charity, or the grace of love, never fails.
V. I shall conclude all with an exhortation to high and low, rich and poor, one with another, to be found in the constant practice of this valuable and commendable duty.
First, I shall consider this duty as it relates to the bodies of men. And,
1. Oh, that the rich would consider how praiseworthy this duty is, in helping their fellow creatures!

We were created to be a help to each other; God has made no one so independent as not to need the assistance of another; the richest and most powerful man on the face of this earth needs the help and assistance of those who are around him; and though he may be great today, a thousand accidents may bring him as low tomorrow; he who is rolling in plenty today may be in as much scarcity tomorrow.

If our rich men would be more charitable to their poor friends and neighbors, it would be a means of recommending them to the favor of others, if Providence should frown on them; but alas, our great men would much rather spend their money at a playhouse, at a ball, an assembly, or a masquerade, than relieve a poor, distressed servant of Jesus Christ.

They would rather spend their estates on their hawks and hounds, on their whores, and on earthly, sensual, devilish pleasures, than comfort, nourish, or relieve one of their distressed fellow creatures.
What difference is there between the king on the throne and the beggar on the dunghill, when God demands their breath?
There is no difference, my brethren, in the grave, nor will there be any on the day of judgment.

You will not be excused because you have had a great estate, a fine house, and lived in all the pleasures that earth could afford you; no, these things will be one means of your condemnation; nor will you be judged according to the size of your estate, but according to the use you have made of it.

Now you may think of nothing but your pleasures and delights, of living in ease and plenty, and never consider how many thousands of your fellow creatures would rejoice at what you are wasting and setting no value on.
Let me implore you, my rich brethren, to consider the poor of the world, and how commendable and praiseworthy it is to relieve those who are distressed.

Consider how pleasing this is to God, how delightful it is to man, and how many prayers will be offered up for your welfare by those persons whom you relieve; and let this be a reason to spare a little out of the abundance with which God has blessed you, for the relief of his poor.

He could have placed you in their low condition, and them in your high state; it is only his good pleasure that has made this difference, and shall this not make you remember your distressed fellow creatures?

Let me implore you to consider which will serve you best on the day of judgment: so much money spent at a horse race or a cockpit, at a play or a masquerade, or so much given for the relief of your fellow creatures and for the distressed members of Jesus Christ.

I implore you to consider how valuable and commendable this duty is: do not be angry at my exhorting you in this way to a duty that is so highly recommended by Jesus Christ himself and by all his apostles: I speak particularly to you, my rich brethren, to entreat you to consider those who are poor in this world, and to help them from time to time, as their need calls for it.

Consider that a curse is pronounced against the riches of those who do not do good with them in this way; namely, “Come now, you rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you; your riches are corrupted, your garments are moth-eaten, your gold and silver are rusted through, and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as though it were fire; you have heaped your treasure together for the last day.”

You see the dreadful woe pronounced against all those who hoard up the abundance of the things of this life without relieving the distress of those who are in want of them: and the apostle James also goes on to speak against those who have acquired estates by fraud, as too many have in these days.

“Behold, the wages of the laborers who have reaped down your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out; and the cries of those who have reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord God of Sabaoth.
You have lived in pleasure on the earth and been wanton; you have nourished your hearts, as in the day of slaughter.”

Thus, if you go on living according to the lust of the flesh, pampering your bellies and making them a god, while the poor all around you are starving, God will make these things a witness against you, which shall be like a worm to your souls and gnaw at your consciences for all eternity; therefore, let me once more recommend charity to the bodies of men, and implore you to remember what the blessed Lord Jesus Christ has promised to those who love his members in this way, that “as they have done it to the least of his members, they have done it to him.”

I am not now speaking for myself; I am not recommending my little flock in Georgia to you; then you might say, as many wantonly do, that I wanted the money for myself; no, my brethren, I am now recommending the poor of this land to you, your poor neighbors, poor friends, yes, your poor enemies; they are the ones I am now speaking for; and when I see so many starving in the streets, and almost naked, my heart is moved with pity and concern to consider that many who have it in their power to lend a helping hand should shut up their hearts of compassion, and will not relieve their fellow creatures, though they are in the most deplorable condition for want of it.
As I have thus recommended charity particularly to the rich among you, so now I would,
2. Secondly, recommend this to another group of people among us, who, instead of being the most forward in acts of charity, are commonly the most backward; I mean the clergy of this land.
Good God! How amazing is the thought that those whom God has called out to labor in spiritual things should be so backward in this duty, as fatal experience teaches.

Our clergy (that is, the majority of them) are only seeking after preferment, running up and down to obtain one benefice after another, and to heap up an estate, either to spend on the pleasures of life or to gratify their sensual appetites, while the poor of their flock are forgotten; no, worse, they are scorned, hated, and disdained.

I am not now, my brethren, speaking of all the clergy; no, blessed be God, there are some among them who abhor such proceedings and are willing to relieve the needy; but God knows these are only very few, while many take no thought of the poor among them.
They can visit the rich and the great, but they cannot bear the poor in their sight; they are forgetful, willfully forgetful, of the poor members of Jesus Christ.

They have left the old paths and turned into a new, polite way, but one which is not warranted in the word of God: they have sunk into a fine way of acting; but fine as it is, it was not the practice of the apostles, or of the Christians in any age of the church: for they visited and relieved the poor among them; but how rare is this among us, how seldom do we find charity in a clergyman?

It is with grief that I speak these things, but woeful experience is a witness to their truth: and if all the clergy of this land were here, I would tell them boldly that they did not keep to the ways of charity, but were remiss in their duty; instead of “selling all and giving to the poor,” they will not sell anything, nor give anything at all to the poor.
3. Thirdly, I would exhort you who are poor to be charitable to one another.

Though you may not have money, or the things of this life, to give to one another, yet you may assist them by comforting them and advising them not to be discouraged, though they are low in the world; or in sickness you may help them as you have time or ability: do not be unkind to one another: do not grieve, or vex, or be angry with each other; for this is giving the world an advantage over you.

And if God stirs up anyone to relieve you, do not make a bad use of what his providence has bestowed on you by the hands of some Christian: be always humble and wait on God; do not murmur or complain if you see others relieved and you are not; still wait on the Lord, and help one another, according to your abilities, from time to time.
Having shown you how valuable this is to the bodies of men, I now proceed,
Secondly, to show you how much more valuable this charity is when it extends to the souls of men.
And is not the soul more valuable than the body?
It would be of no advantage, but an infinite disadvantage, to gain the whole world if we were to lose our souls.

The soul is of infinite value and of infinite concern, and therefore we should extend our charity whenever we see it needed, and should likewise reprove, rebuke, and exhort with all godliness and love.
We should, my dear brethren, use all means and opportunities for the salvation of our own souls and of the souls of others.

We may have a great deal of charity and concern for the bodies of our fellow creatures when we have no thought or concern for their immortal souls: but oh, how sad it is to have thought for the mortal but not for the immortal part; to have charity for the body of our fellow creatures while we have no concern for their immortal souls; it may be that we help them toward their ruin, but have no concern for their salvation.

You may love to spend a merry evening, or go to a play or a horse race, with them; but on the other hand, you cannot bear the thought of going to a sermon or a religious society with them; no, you would sing the songs of the drunkard with them, but you will not sing hymns with them; this is not polite enough, this is unbecoming a gentleman of taste, unfashionable, and practiced only among a pack of fanatics and madmen.

Thus you will be so uncharitable as to join hand in hand with those who are hurrying to their own damnation, while you will not be so charitable as to help them be brought from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God.

But this, this, my dear brethren, is the greatest charity there can be, to save a soul from death: this is of far greater advantage than relieving the body of a fellow creature: for as to the most miserable object that could be, death would deliver it from everything.
But death, to those who are not born again, would be so far from being a release from all misery that it would be an entrance into all torment, and that for all eternity.
Therefore we should do all we possibly can to keep a soul from falling into the hands of Satan: for he is the great enemy of souls.
How much should this stir you to watch over your own souls and the souls of others?
For unless you are earnest with God, Satan will be too strong for you.
Surely it is the greatest charity to watch over one another's words and actions, so that we may warn each other beforehand when danger is near, or when the enemy of souls approaches.
And if you have once known the value of your own souls, and know what it is to be snatched like brands out of the burning fire, you will be eager that others may be brought out of the same state.

It is not the leading of a moral life, being honest, and paying every man his just due; this is not a proof of your being in a state of grace, or of being born again and renewed in the spirit of your minds: no, you may die honest, just, charitable, and yet not be in a state of salvation.
It is not the preaching of that morality which most of our pulpits now bring forth that is sufficient to bring you from sin to God.

I saw you willing to learn, and yet ignorant of the necessity of being born again, regenerated, of having all old things done away and all things becoming new in your souls: I could not bear, my brethren, to see you on the highway to destruction, with no one to bring you back.
It was love for your souls, it was a desire to see Christ formed in you, that brought me into the fields, the highways, and hedges, to preach Jesus to you, a crucified Jesus, dying for you.
It was charity, indeed it was charity to your souls, that has exposed me to the present ill treatment from my letter-learned brethren.

Therefore, let me advise you to be charitable to one another's souls; that is, by advising them with all love and tenderness to follow after Christ and the things which belong to their immortal peace, before they are forever hidden from their eyes.
I now proceed, in the third place, to show when your charity is of the right kind.
And here, my brethren, I shall show, first, when it is not; and secondly, when it is of the right kind.
1. First, your charity is not of the right kind when it proceeds from worldly views or ends.

If it is to be seen by men, to receive any advantage from them, to be esteemed, or to gain a reputation in the world; or if you take any pride in it, and expect to reap benefit from God merely for it; if all or any of these is the end of your charity, then it is all in vain; your charity does not proceed from a right end, but you are thereby deceiving your own souls.

If you give alms purely to be observed by men, or expecting favor from God merely on account of it, then you do not have the glory of God or the benefit of your fellow creatures at heart, but merely yourself: this, this is not charity. Nor,

Secondly, is it true charity when we give anything to our fellow creatures purely to indulge them in vice: this is so far from being charity that it is a sin, both against God and against our fellow creatures.
And yet it is as common as it is sinful to take our friends, under a specious pretense of charity, to one entertainment or another, with no other aim than to make them guilty of excess.
By this you are guilty of a double sin: we are not to sin ourselves, much less should we try to make another sin as well. But,
Thirdly, our charity comes from a right end when it proceeds from love to God, and for the welfare of both the body and soul of our fellow creatures.

When this is the sole end of relieving our distressed fellow creatures, then our charity comes from a right end, and we may expect to reap benefit from it: this is the charity which is pleasing to God.
God is well pleased when all our actions proceed from love, love to himself and love to immortal souls.

Consider, my dear brethren, that it was love for souls that brought the blessed Jesus down from the bosom of his Father; that made him, who was equal in power and glory, come and take our nature upon himself; that caused the Lord of life to die the painful, ignominious, and accursed death of the cross.
It was love for immortal souls that brought this blessed Jesus among us.
And oh, that we might consider from this how great the value of souls was and is: it was this that made Jesus bleed, pant, and die.
And surely souls must be of infinite worth, which made the Lamb of God die so shameful a death.
And shall this not make you truly value souls?
The soul is of the greatest worth: and this, this is the greatest charity, when it comes from love to God and from love to souls.
This will be a charity whose satisfaction will last for all eternity.

Oh, that this may give you so much regard for the value of souls that you will not neglect any opportunity of doing them good: here is something worth having charity for, because they remain for all eternity.

Therefore, let me earnestly implore you both to consider the worth of immortal souls and to let your charity extend to them, so that by your advice and admonition you may be an instrument in the hands of God in bringing souls to the Lord Jesus.
I am next to consider, fourthly, why this charity, or grace of love, never fails.
And it never fails in that it proceeds from an unchangeable God.
We are not to understand that our charity is always the same: no, there may be, and frequently are, ebbs and flows; but still it never fails completely: no, the grace of love remains forever.
There is, and will be, a charity toward all who have erred and gone astray from God.
We cannot be at ease seeing souls on the highway to destruction without using our utmost endeavor to bring them back from sin and to show them the dreadful consequence of running into evil.

Christians cannot bear to see those souls for whom Christ died perish for lack of knowledge: and if they see the bodies of any of their fellow creatures in want, they will do the utmost in their power to relieve them.
Charity will never fail among those who have a true love for the Lord Jesus and know the value of souls: they will be charitable to those who are in distress.
And so you see that true charity, if it proceeds from a right end, never fails.
I now proceed, my brethren, in the last place, to exhort all of you, high and low, rich and poor, one with another, to practice this valuable and commendable duty of charity.

It is not rolling along in your coaches, taking your pleasure, and not considering the miseries of your fellow creatures, that is commendable or praiseworthy; but relieving your distressed, poor fellow creatures is valuable and praiseworthy wherever it is found.
But alas! how very few of our fashionable and polite gentlemen consider their poor friends; rather, they despise them and do not regard them.

They can indulge themselves in the follies of life, and would much rather spend their estates on lusts and pleasures, while the poor all around them are not thought worthy to be set with the dogs of their flock.

If you have an abundance of the things of this world, then you are esteemed as a companion for the polite and fashionable in life; but if you are poor, then you must not expect to find any favor, but to be hated, or not thought fit for company or conversation: and if you have an abundance of the things of this life, and do not need any assistance, then you have many ready to help you.

My dear brethren, I do not doubt that your own experience is a proof of what I assert; as also that, if anyone comes into distress, then those who promised to give relief quite forget what they promised, and will despise him, because Providence has frowned.

But this is not acting like those who are bound for the heavenly Jerusalem; thus our hearts and our actions give the lie to our lips: for if we profess the name of Christ and do not depart from all iniquity, we are not those who are worthy of being esteemed Christians indeed.
For if we do not have charity, we are not Christians: charity is the great duty of Christians: and where is our Christianity if we lack charity?
Therefore, let me implore you to exercise charity toward your distressed fellow creatures.

Indeed, my dear brethren, this is truly commendable, truly valuable; and therefore I implore you, with hearts of tender mercy toward Christ, to consider his poor, distressed members; exercise, exercise, I implore you, this charity: if you have no compassion, you are not true disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ.
I humbly beg you to consider those who need relief and are truly destitute, and to relieve them according to your abilities.

Consider that the more favorable Providence has been to you, the more earnest and eager it should make you to relieve those whom you may find in distress: it is of the utmost consequence, both what is well pleasing to your fellow creatures and the doing of your duty to God.

When you are called from here, then all riches and grandeur will be over; the grave will make no distinction; great estates will be of no significance in the other world; and if you have made a bad use of the talent which God has put into your hands, it will only aggravate your condemnation on the great day of account, when God shall come to demand your souls and to call you to account for the use to which you have put the abundance of the things of this life.
To conclude, let me once more implore each of you to act according to the circumstances of life which God, in his rich and free mercy, has given you.

If you were aware of the great consequences that would attend your acting in this charitable manner, and considered it a proof of your love to God, the loving of his members, you could not be uncharitable in your disposition, nor fail to relieve any of your distressed fellow creatures.

Consider how easy it is for many of you, by putting your mites together, to help one who is in distress; and how can you tell but that the little you give may be the means of bringing someone from distress into flourishing circumstances; and then, if there is a true Christian spirit in them, they can never be thankful enough to God the author, and to you as the instrument, for being so great a friend to them in their sad circumstances: consider also, once more, how much better your account will be on the day of judgment, and what peace of conscience you will enjoy.
How satisfying must the thought be of having relieved the widow and the fatherless?
This is recommended by the Lord Jesus Christ, and has been practiced in all ages of the church: and therefore, my brethren, be found now in the practice of this duty.

I have spoken at greater length on this because our enemies say we deny all moral actions; but, blessed be God, they speak against us without cause: we highly value them; but we say that faith in Christ, the love of God, and being born again are of infinitely more worth; but you cannot be true Christians without having charity toward your fellow creatures, whether they are friends or enemies, if they are in distress.
And therefore exert yourselves in this duty, as the blessed Jesus has commanded: and if you have true charity, you shall live and reign with him forever.
Now to God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, be all honor, power, glory, might, majesty, and dominion, both now and forevermore. Amen.
Genesis 3:15 — “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; it shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.”
In reading these words to you, I may address you in the language of the holy angels to the shepherds who were watching their flocks by night: “Behold, I bring you glad tidings of great joy.”
For this is the first promise of a Savior that was made to the apostate race of Adam.
We generally look for Christ only in the New Testament; but Christianity, in one sense, is very nearly as old as the creation.
It is wonderful to observe how gradually God revealed his Son to mankind.
He began with the promise in the text, and on this the elect lived until the time of Abraham.
To him God made further disclosures of his eternal counsel concerning man’s redemption.
Afterward, at different times and in different manners, God spoke to the fathers by the prophets, until at length the Lord Jesus himself was manifested in the flesh, and came and dwelt among us.

This first promise must certainly have been only dim to our first parents, compared with the great light that we enjoy. And yet, dim as it was, we may be sure that they built upon it their hopes of everlasting salvation, and by that faith were saved.
How they came to need this promise, and what its extent and meaning are, I intend, God willing, to make the subject of your present meditation.
The fall of man is written in characters too legible not to be understood: those who deny it prove it by their very denial.
Even the heathen confessed and lamented it: they could see the streams of corruption running through the whole race of mankind, but could not trace them to the fountainhead.
Before God gave a revelation of his Son, man was a riddle to himself.
And Moses unfolds more in this one chapter (from which the text is taken) than all mankind could have found out by themselves, even if they had studied for all eternity.

In the preceding chapter he had given us a full account of how God spoke the world into being, and especially how he formed man from the dust of the earth and breathed into him the breath of life, so that he became a living soul.
A council of the Trinity was called concerning the formation of this lovely creature.
The result of that council was, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
So God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him.”
Moses remarkably repeats these words, so that we might take particular notice of our divine origin.
Never was so much expressed in so few words: no one but an inspired man could have done it.

But it is remarkable that, though Moses mentions our being made in the image of God, he mentions it only twice, and then only in passing; as though he would have said, “Man was made in honor; God made him upright; ‘in the image of God, male and female he created them.’
But man fell so soon, and became like the beasts that perish, indeed, like the devil himself, that it is hardly worth mentioning.”
How soon man fell after he was created is not told us; and therefore to fix any time is to be wise beyond what is written.
And I think those who suppose that man fell on the same day in which he was made have no sufficient ground for their opinion.

The many things crowded together in the previous chapter, such as the forming of Adam’s wife, his naming of the beasts, and his being placed in the garden which God had planted, I think require a longer span of time than one day to be carried out.
However, all agree on this: “man did not stand long.”
How long, or how short a time, I will not take it upon myself to determine.
It concerns us more to inquire how he came to fall from his steadfastness, and what was the origin and progress of the temptation that prevailed over him.
The account this chapter gives of it is very full; and it may do us much good, under God, to make some remarks on it.

“Now the serpent (says the sacred historian) was more subtle than any beast of the field that the Lord God had made, and he said to the woman, Yes, has God said, you shall not eat of every tree of the garden?”

Though this was a real serpent, yet the one who spoke was none other than the devil; perhaps for this reason he is called the old serpent, because he took possession of the serpent when he came to deceive our first parents.
The devil envied the happiness of man, who was made, as some think, to fill the place of the fallen angels.
God made man upright, and with full power to stand if he chose: he was just, therefore, in allowing him to be tempted.
If he fell, he had no one to blame but himself.
But how is Satan to bring about his fall?

He cannot do it by his power, so he attempts it by cunning: he takes possession of a serpent, which was more subtle than all the beasts of the field that the Lord God had made; so that men who are full of subtlety but have no piety are only machines for the devil to work upon, just as he pleases.
“And he said to the woman.”
Here is an example of his subtlety.
He speaks to the woman, the weaker vessel, and when she was apart from her husband and therefore more liable to be overcome: “Yes, has God said, you shall not eat of every tree of the garden?”
These words are certainly spoken in answer to something the devil either saw or heard.

In all probability the woman was now near the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (for we shall soon find her plucking an apple from it); perhaps she was looking at it, and wondering what there was in that tree more than in the others, that she and her husband should be forbidden to take of it.

Satan, seeing this, and eager to draw her into a parley with him (for if the devil can persuade us not to resist him, but to converse with him, he has gained a great point), says, “Yes, has God said, you shall not eat of every tree in the garden?”

The first thing he does is to persuade her, if possible, to entertain hard thoughts of God; this is his usual way of dealing with God’s children: “Yes, has God said, you shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
What! Has God planted a garden, and placed you in the middle of it, only to tease and perplex you?
Has he planted a garden, and yet forbidden you to make use of any of its fruits at all?”
It was impossible for him to ask a more ensnaring question in order to gain his end: for Eve was here seemingly obliged to answer and to defend God’s goodness.
And therefore —
Verses 2 and 3.

The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden; but of the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the garden, God has said, you shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.”
The first part of the answer was good: “We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden; God has not forbidden us to eat of every tree of the garden.

No; we may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden (and, it would seem, even of the tree of life, which was like a sacrament to man in the state of innocence); there is only one tree in the middle of the garden of which God has said, you shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.”
Here she begins to swerve, and sin begins to be conceived in her heart.
Already she has taken in some of the serpent’s poison by talking with him, which she ought not to have done at all.
For she might easily have supposed that it could be no good being who would put such a question to her and insinuate such dishonorable thoughts of God.
She should therefore have fled from him, and not stayed to parley with him at all.
Immediately the ill effects of it appear: she begins to soften the divine threat.
God had said, “In the day you eat of it, you shall surely die”; or, dying you shall die.
But Eve says, “You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.”

We may be sure that we have fallen into temptation, and are beginning to fall by it, when we begin to think that God will not be as good as his word with regard to carrying out the threats he has pronounced against sin.
Satan knew this, and therefore cunningly
“Said to the woman (verse 4), You shall not surely die,” in an insinuating manner, “You shall not surely die.
Surely God will not be so cruel as to damn you merely for eating an apple; it cannot be.”

Alas! How many does Satan lead captive at his will by flattering them that they shall not surely die; that the torments of hell will not be eternal; that God is all mercy; that he therefore will not punish a few years of sin with an eternity of misery?
But Eve found God as good as his word; and so will all those who go on in sin under a false hope that they shall not surely die.
We may also take the words as spoken positively, and this agrees with what follows: You shall not surely die; “It is all a delusion, a mere bugbear, to keep you in servile subjection.”
For (verse 5) “God knows that on the day you eat of it, then your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”
What child of God can expect to escape slander, when God himself was slandered like this even in paradise?
Surely Eve’s understanding must have been blinded in some measure, or she would not have allowed the tempter to speak such perverse things.
In what hateful colors God is represented here!
“God knows that on the day you eat of it, you shall be as gods” (equal with God).
So the grand temptation was that they would thereafter be under no control, equal to, if not above, the God who made them, knowing good and evil.
Eve could not tell what Satan meant by this; but she certainly understood it to mean some great privilege they were to enjoy.
And so Satan now points out a way that seems right to sinners, but does not tell them that the end of that way is death.

To give strength and force to this temptation, in all probability Satan, or the serpent, at this time plucked an apple from the tree and ate it in front of Eve; by which Eve might be led to think that the shrewdness and power of speech the serpent had above the other beasts must be owing, in large measure, to his eating that fruit; and therefore, if he had gained so much improvement, she might also expect a like benefit from it.
All this, I think, is clear; for otherwise I do not see how it could fittingly be said, “When the woman saw that it was good for food.”
How could she know it was good for food, unless she had seen the serpent feed on it?
Satan now begins to gain ground quickly.
Lust had conceived in Eve’s heart; soon it will bring forth sin.
Sin, once conceived, brings forth death.

Verse 6: “And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit of it and ate, and gave also to her husband, and he ate.”
Our senses are the landing ports of our spiritual enemies.
How necessary is that resolution of holy Job, “I have made a covenant with my eyes!”
When Eve began to gaze on the forbidden fruit with her eyes, she soon began to long for it with her heart.

When she saw that it was good for food, and pleasant to the eyes (here was the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eye), but, above all, a tree to be desired to make one wise, wiser than God would have her be, indeed, as wise as God himself, she took of the fruit of it, and gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.
As soon as she had sinned herself, she turned tempter to her husband.
It is dreadful when those who should be helpers to each other in the great work of their salvation are only promoters of each other’s damnation: but so it is.
If we ourselves are good, we shall stir others to goodness; if we do evil, we shall entice others to do evil also.
There is a close connection between doing and teaching.

How necessary, then, is it for all of us to take care that we do not sin in any way ourselves, lest we become agents for the devil and ensnare, perhaps, our nearest and dearest relatives? “She gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.”
Alas! What a complication of crimes there was in this one single act of sin!
Here is an utter disbelief of God’s threat; the utmost ingratitude to their Maker, who had so recently planted this garden and placed them in it with such a glorious and comprehensive charter.
And the utmost neglect of their descendants, who they knew were to stand or fall with them.
Here was the utmost pride of heart: they wanted to be equal with God.
Here is the utmost contempt heaped upon his threat and his law: the devil is believed and obeyed before him, and all this only to satisfy their sensual appetite.
Never was a crime of such a complicated nature committed by anyone here below: nothing but the devil’s apostasy and rebellion could equal it.
And what are the consequences of their disobedience?
Are their eyes opened?
Yes, their eyes are opened; but, alas!
It is only to see their own nakedness.
For we are told (verse 7) “that the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.”
Naked of God, naked of everything that was holy and good, and stripped of the divine image which they had enjoyed before.
They might rightly now be called Ichabod; for the glory of the Lord had departed from them.
O how low these sons of the morning then fell!
Out of God, into themselves; from being partakers of the divine nature, into the nature of the devil and the beast.
Well, therefore, might they know that they were naked, not only in body but in soul.
And how do they behave now that they are naked?
Do they flee to God for pardon?
Do they seek from God a robe to cover their nakedness?

No, they were now dead to God, and had become earthly, sensual, devilish: therefore, instead of turning to God for mercy, “they sewed or plaited fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons,” or things to gird about them.

This is a vivid picture of every natural man: we see that we are naked; we confess it in some measure; but instead of looking up to God for help, we patch together a righteousness of our own (as our first parents plaited fig leaves together), hoping to cover our nakedness with that.
But our righteousness will not withstand the severity of God’s judgment: it will do us no more good than the fig leaves did Adam and Eve, that is, none at all.

For (verse 8) “They heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the trees of the garden in the cool of the day; and Adam and his wife (despite their fig leaves) hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.”
They heard the voice of the Lord God, or the Word of the Lord God, even the Lord Jesus Christ, who is “the Word that was with God, and the Word that was God.”
They heard him walking in the trees of the garden in the cool of the day.
A time, perhaps, when Adam and Eve used to go in a special manner and offer up an evening sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving.
The cool of the day.
Perhaps the sin was committed early in the morning, or at noon; but God would not come upon them immediately; he waited until the cool of the day.
And if we want to reprove others effectively, we should not do it when they are heated with passion, but wait until the cool of the day.
But what a change is here!
Instead of rejoicing at the voice of their beloved, instead of meeting him with open arms and enlarged hearts as before, they now hide themselves in the trees of the garden.
Alas, what a foolish attempt this was!
Surely they must have been naked; otherwise how could they think of hiding themselves from God?
Where could they flee from his presence?
But by their fall they had taken on an enmity against God: they now hated God their Maker, and were afraid to converse with him.
And is this not our condition by nature?

Assuredly it is. We labor to cover our nakedness with the fig leaves of our own righteousness: we hide ourselves from God as long as we can, and will not come, and never would come, if the Father did not go before us, draw us, and sweetly constrain us by his grace, as he here went before Adam.
Verse 9. “And the Lord God called to Adam, and said to him, Adam, where are you?”
“The Lord God called to Adam” (for otherwise Adam would never have called to the Lord God), and said, “Adam, where are you?
How is it that you do not come to pay your devotions as usual?”
Christians, remember that the Lord keeps an account when you fail to come to worship.
Whenever, therefore, you are tempted to withhold your attendance, let each of you imagine that you hear the Lord calling to you and saying, “O man, O woman, where are you?”
It may be understood in another and better sense: “Adam, where are you?”
What condition is your poor soul in?

This is the first thing the Lord asks a sinner and convinces him of, when he goes before him and calls him effectually by his grace; he also calls him by name; for unless God speaks to us in particular, and we know where we are, how poor, how miserable, how blind, how naked, we shall never value the redemption accomplished for us by the death and obedience of the dear Lord Jesus.
“Adam, where are you?”
Verse 10. “And he said, I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid.”
See what cowards sin makes of us.
If we knew no sin, we would know no fear.
“Because I was naked, and I hid myself.”
Verse 11: “And he said, Who told you that you were naked?
Have you eaten of the tree that I (your Maker and Lawgiver) commanded you not to eat of?”
God knew very well that Adam was naked, and that he had eaten of the forbidden fruit; but God would hear it from Adam’s own mouth.
In the same way God knows all our needs before we ask, and yet insists that we ask for his grace and confess our sins.
For by such acts we acknowledge our dependence on God, take shame to ourselves, and so give glory to his great name.
Verse 12. “And the man said, The woman that you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I ate.”
Never was human nature more vividly portrayed.
See what pride Adam took on by the fall!
How unwilling he is to lay the blame on himself, or take shame to himself.
This answer is full of insolence toward God, hostility against his wife, and dishonesty with regard to himself.
For in it he tacitly casts reproach on God.
“The woman that you gave to be with me.”
As much as to say, if you had not given me that woman, I would not have eaten the forbidden fruit.
So, when men sin, they lay the fault on their passions, and then blame and cast reproach on God for giving them those passions.
Their language is, “The appetites that you gave us, they deceived us; and therefore we sinned against you.”
But as God nevertheless punished Adam for listening to the voice of his wife, so he will punish those who listen to the dictates of their corrupt inclinations.
For God compels no one to sin.
Adam could have withstood his wife’s urging, if he had wished.
And so, if we look up to God, we would find grace to help in time of need.
The devil and our own hearts tempt us, but they cannot force us to consent without the agreement of our own wills.
So our damnation is of our own making, as will plainly appear on the great day, despite all men’s present shameless answers against God.
As Adam speaks insolently with regard to God, so he speaks with hostility against his wife: the woman, or this woman, she gave me.
He lays all the fault on her, and speaks of her with great contempt.
He does not say, my wife, my dear wife; but, this woman.
Sin divides the most united hearts: it is the bane of holy fellowship.
Those who have been companions in sin here, if they die without repentance, will both hate and condemn one another hereafter.
All damned souls are accusers of their brothers.
So it is, to some degree, on this side of the grave.
“The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I ate.”
What a disingenuous speech this was!
He uses no fewer than fifteen words to excuse himself, and only one or two (in the original) to confess his fault, if it may be called a confession at all.
“The woman that you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree”; here are fifteen words; “and I ate.”
With what reluctance do these last words come out?
How quickly are they spoken?
“And I ate.”
But so it is with an unhumbled, unregenerate heart: it will lay the fault on the dearest friend in the world, indeed on God himself, rather than take shame to itself.
We are all subject to this pride by the fall; and until our hearts are broken and made contrite by the Spirit of our Lord Jesus Christ, we shall always be charging God foolishly.

“Against you, and you only, have I sinned, that you might be justified in your saying, and clear when you are judged,” is the language of none but those who, like David, are willing to confess their faults and are truly sorry for their sins.

This was not the case with Adam; his heart was not broken; and therefore he lays the fault of his disobedience on his wife and on God, and not on himself: “The woman that you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I ate.”
Verse 13. “And the Lord God said, What is this that you have done?”
What wonderful concern God expresses in this remonstrance!
“What a flood of misery have you brought upon yourself, your husband, and your descendants?
What is this that you have done?
Disobeyed your God, obeyed the devil, and ruined your husband, for whom I made you to be a helper!
What is this that you have done?”
God would here awaken her to a sense of her crime and danger, and therefore, as it were, thunders in her ears: for the law must be preached to self-righteous sinners.
We must beware of healing before we see sinners wounded, lest we should say, Peace, peace, where there is no peace.
Complacent sinners must hear the thunderings of Mount Sinai before we bring them to Mount Zion.
Those who never preach the law, it is to be feared, are unskilled in delivering the glad tidings of the gospel.
Every minister should be a Boanerges, a son of thunder, as well as a Barnabas, a son of consolation.
There was an earthquake and a whirlwind before the small still voice came to Elijah: we must first show people that they are condemned, and then show them how they must be saved.
But how and when to preach the law, and when to apply the promises of the gospel, wisdom is profitable to direct.
“And the Lord God said to the woman, What is this that you have done?”
“And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I ate.”
She does not use as many words to excuse herself as her husband did; but her heart is as unhumbled as his.
What is this, says God, that you have done?
God here charges her with doing it.
She dares not deny the fact, or say, I have not done it; but she takes all the blame off herself and lays it on the serpent: “The serpent beguiled me, and I ate.”

She does not say, “Lord, I was to blame for talking with the serpent; Lord, I did wrong in not hurrying to my husband when he put the first question to me; Lord, I plead guilty, I alone am to blame; O let not my poor husband suffer for my wickedness!”
This would have been the language of her heart had she now been a true penitent.
But both were now equally proud; therefore neither will lay the blame on themselves: “The serpent beguiled me, and I ate.
The woman that you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I ate.”
I have been the more detailed in remarking on this part of their behavior because it tends so much to magnify free grace, and plainly shows us that salvation comes only from the Lord.
Let us take a short look at the miserable circumstances our first parents were now in: they were legally and spiritually dead, children of wrath, and heirs of hell.
They had eaten the fruit of which God had commanded them that they should not eat; and when arraigned before God, although their crime was so complicated, they could not be brought to confess it.
What reason can be given why the sentence of death should not be pronounced against the prisoners at the bar?
All must admit that they deserve to die.
Indeed, how can God, consistently with his justice, possibly forgive them?
He had threatened that in the day they ate of the forbidden fruit they should “surely die”; and if he did not carry out this threat, the devil might then slander the Almighty indeed.
And yet mercy cries, Spare these sinners, spare the work of your own hands.
Behold, then, wisdom devises a plan by which God may be just and yet be merciful; be faithful to his threat, punish the offense, and at the same time spare the offender.
An amazing scene of divine love here opens to our view, which had been hidden in the heart of God from all eternity!
Although Adam and Eve were so unhumbled, and did not offer so much as one single petition for pardon, God immediately passes sentence on the serpent and reveals to them a Savior.

Verse 14. “And the Lord God said to the serpent, Because you have done this, you are cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life”; that is, he should be in subjection, and his power should always be limited and restrained.
“His enemies shall lick the very dust,” says the Psalmist.
(Verse 15.) “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed: it shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.”

Before I go on to explain this verse, I cannot help noticing one great mistake of which the author of The Whole Duty of Man is guilty, in making this verse contain a covenant between God and Adam, as though God now dealt with Adam personally, as before the fall.
